instruction: Before I can run `helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher`, Helm says the repo 'rancher-prime' is not found. How do I fix that?
reference: Helm does not know the repository yet. Add it with `helm repo add rancher-prime <helm-chart-repo-url>`, using the repository URL from the Prime-only documentation (log in with your SUSE Customer Center credentials), then run `helm repo update` and retry the install.

instruction: Our install runbook has a step 'create the namespace for the Rancher server'. What exactly should that step run?
reference: It should run `kubectl create namespace cattle-system`. The Rancher chart's resources should always be installed in `cattle-system`, with the Helm release named `rancher`.

instruction: I'm doing a proof of concept at rancher.lab.example and I'm fine with Rancher creating its own CA. Write the Helm command I should start from.
reference: Start from the documented command `helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system --set hostname=rancher.my.org --set bootstrapPassword=admin` and change `hostname` to `rancher.lab.example` and `bootstrapPassword` to a unique value. No `ingress.tls.source` is needed because `rancher` (Rancher-generated certificates, issued through cert-manager) is the default.
expect_command: helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system --set hostname=rancher.my.org --set bootstrapPassword=admin

instruction: Our security team will hand us a certificate signed by our corporate CA. Which ingress.tls.source should we use, and can we skip cert-manager?
reference: Use `ingress.tls.source=secret`, which uses certificates from files. cert-manager is not required for this option. Because the certificate is signed by a private CA, also set `privateCA=true` and upload the CA certificate as described in Adding TLS Secrets.

instruction: In my CI pipeline I want a step that blocks until the Rancher server deployment is fully available after `helm upgrade`. What command do I use?
reference: Use `kubectl -n cattle-system rollout status deploy/rancher`. It waits until the `rancher` deployment in `cattle-system` reports a successful rollout.

instruction: A teammate installed Rancher last night and went on holiday without telling anyone the first-login password. I have kubeconfig for the local cluster. How do I get in?
reference: If no bootstrap password was set, Rancher generated one and stored it in `bootstrap-secret` in `cattle-system`. Print it with `kubectl get secret --namespace cattle-system bootstrap-secret -o go-template='{{ .data.bootstrapPassword|base64decode}}{{ "\n" }}'`, log in as admin, and set a new password when prompted.
expect_command: kubectl get secret --namespace cattle-system bootstrap-secret -o go-template='{{ .data.bootstrapPassword|base64decode}}{{ "\n" }}'

instruction: The only person who knew the Rancher admin password left the company. Rancher runs on our three-node RKE2 cluster. What do I run to get a new admin password?
reference: Use the `reset-password` tool inside a Rancher pod. With `KUBECONFIG` set to the RKE2 cluster's kubeconfig, run `kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password`. It prints a new password for the default administrator.
expect_command: kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password

instruction: Someone removed every admin account from our Rancher server and now nobody can manage users. Which in-pod tool restores an administrator, and how do I run it?
reference: Use `ensure-default-admin`. With `KUBECONFIG` pointing at the Rancher server cluster, run `kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher | grep '1/1' | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -- ensure-default-admin`. It prints a new default administrator and its password.
expect_command: kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher | grep '1/1' | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -- ensure-default-admin

instruction: Management wants our Rancher jump from an older 2.11 patch to the newest release in a single maintenance window. What upgrade sequence do the docs actually support?
reference: Upgrade one minor version at a time. First move to the latest patch of 2.11, then to the latest patch of 2.12, and so on, each time from the latest patch of the current minor to the latest patch of the next. This is the only tested and supported path between minor versions.

instruction: I need to pick a --version for my Rancher upgrade but don't know what's published. How do I list what's in the repo?
reference: Run `helm repo update`, then `helm search repo rancher-prime/rancher --versions` to list all published chart versions, and choose the version for your upgrade from that list.

instruction: We're migrating Rancher to new hardware and want the new install to use the same chart settings as the current one. How do I capture them from the running server?
reference: With kubeconfig pointing at the current Rancher cluster, run `helm get values rancher -n cattle-system -o yaml > values.yaml`. Then use that file with `-f` when you run the Helm command on the new environment.
expect_command: helm get values rancher -n cattle-system -o yaml > values.yaml

instruction: I have values.yaml exported and need to move Rancher to the next patch release without touching any other setting. What's the exact Helm invocation?
reference: Run `helm upgrade rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system -f values.yaml --version={current-patch-version}`, setting the version to the patch you are moving to. The `-f values.yaml` keeps your existing chart values.
expect_command: helm upgrade rancher rancher-prime/rancher --namespace cattle-system -f values.yaml --version={current-patch-version}

instruction: Write me a short pre-flight checklist for a Rancher minor upgrade, based on the official procedure.
reference: 1) Take a backup with the Rancher Backups application, to use as a restore point. 2) Make sure you are on the latest patch of your current minor release. 3) Review installed feature charts under Apps, Installed Apps, and upgrade them to the latest version within their current release line. 4) Review known issues in the release notes. 5) Save your current Helm values.

instruction: We upgraded Rancher yesterday and a critical integration broke. We did take a rancher-backup beforehand. What's the supported way to get back to the old version?
reference: Use the backup. Restore it with the Rancher Backups application by creating a Restore custom resource on the local cluster, then run Rancher at the previous version, for example `helm rollback rancher -n cattle-system`. Changing the version with Helm or kubectl alone is not supported. The target version must still be under active support.

instruction: The Restore resource from our pre-upgrade backup shows Completed. Rancher is still on the new chart version. What Helm command finishes the rollback?
reference: Run `helm rollback rancher -n cattle-system` to return the release to the previous revision. Use `helm history rancher -n cattle-system` if you need to choose a specific revision.

instruction: A project owner on a downstream cluster asks why they can't find a 'Rancher Backups' menu to protect their team's apps. How do I explain it?
reference: Rancher Backups (the rancher-backup operator) runs only on the local cluster that hosts the Rancher server, and it only backs up the Rancher application, not downstream workloads. Only Rancher admins and the local cluster's cluster-owner can use it, so a downstream project owner will not see it.

instruction: I want to automate Rancher backups from a GitOps repo instead of clicking in the UI. What kind of object do I commit?
reference: Commit a `Backup` custom resource (`apiVersion: resources.cattle.io/v1`, kind `Backup`) with the storage location, the `resourceSetName` and, optionally, a `schedule`. The rancher-backup operator on the local cluster acts on it and writes a .tar.gz backup file.

instruction: I'm reviewing a colleague's Backup YAML and it says resourceSetName: rancher-resource-set-basic for our production Rancher. Is that OK?
reference: No, change it to `rancher-resource-set-full`. The basic set excludes secrets, so it does not capture public API tokens (secret-backed since Rancher 2.13), and the docs say it is no longer suitable for production. Use the full set with an encryption config secret so the secrets are encrypted in the backup.

instruction: During a migration the new cluster's Restore needs encryptionConfigSecretName: encryptionconfig, but that secret only existed on the old cluster. I still have the YAML file. How do I recreate it?
reference: Save the EncryptionConfiguration as `encryption-provider-config.yaml` and run `kubectl create secret generic encryptionconfig --from-file=./encryption-provider-config.yaml -n cattle-resources-system` on the new cluster. The key must be `encryption-provider-config.yaml` in the `cattle-resources-system` namespace, and its contents must match the configuration used for the backup.
expect_command: kubectl create secret generic encryptionconfig --from-file=./encryption-provider-config.yaml -n cattle-resources-system

instruction: We use an on-prem MinIO for Rancher backups and the operator logs say access denied. How should the credential secret be built?
reference: The secret must contain the keys `accessKey` and `secretKey`. Create it with `kubectl create secret generic s3-creds --from-literal=accessKey=<access key> --from-literal=secretKey=<secret key>` (filled with your MinIO keys), then point the S3 storage location at it with `credentialSecretName` and `credentialSecretNamespace`.
expect_command: kubectl create secret generic s3-creds --from-literal=accessKey=<access key> --from-literal=secretKey=<secret key>

instruction: Our rancher-backup chart was reinstalled during an upgrade and all backups on the volume vanished. What setting should we have used to prevent that?
reference: Use a StorageClass or persistent volume with a reclaim policy of `Retain`. With any other policy, deleting the PVC created by the rancher-backup chart (for example during an app upgrade) also deletes the PV and every backup on it. If your StorageClass cannot provide Retain, edit the PV's reclaim policy after it is provisioned.

instruction: I kicked off an in-place restore with kubectl and want to see live output from the component doing the work. What do I run?
reference: Follow the rancher-backup operator logs with `kubectl logs -n cattle-resources-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rancher-backup -f`.

instruction: I need to tell users how long the Rancher UI will be down during tonight's restore and why. What actually happens to the Rancher server while the restore runs?
reference: The rancher-backup operator scales down the Rancher deployment when the restore starts and scales it back up once the restore completes. The UI is unavailable for the whole restore. The operator restores CRDs first, then cluster-scoped resources, then namespaced resources.

instruction: I'm writing a Restore manifest for a backup called backup-xyz.tar.gz.enc from our S3 bucket. Which spec fields matter beyond the storage location?
reference: Set `backupFilename: backup-xyz.tar.gz.enc` (the exact file name). Because the file has the `.enc` suffix, set `encryptionConfigSecretName` to a secret in `cattle-resources-system` with the same encryption config used for the backup. `prune` is enabled by default and recommended for an in-place restore. For a migration to a new cluster it must be `false`.

instruction: We plan to move Rancher from an old K3s cluster to a new RKE2 cluster and give it a nicer new URL at the same time. Any problem with that plan?
reference: Yes. A migration must keep the same hostname as the original server URL. Otherwise downstream clusters show as unavailable. Also, do not install Rancher on the new cluster before restoring, set `prune: false` in the Restore, and, because you are changing distributions (K3s to RKE2), edit the local cluster object before bringing Rancher up.

instruction: helm install rancher-charts/rancher-backup fails with 'repo rancher-charts not found' on my fresh migration target. Fix?
reference: Add the repository first: `helm repo add rancher-charts https://charts.rancher.io`, then `helm repo update`, and install the `rancher-backup-crd` chart before `rancher-backup`.

instruction: Script the Helm steps for installing the Rancher backup operator on a cluster that has no Rancher yet (repo already added).
reference: First set CHART_VERSION to a supported version, for example `CHART_VERSION=<chart-version>`. Then run `helm install rancher-backup-crd rancher-charts/rancher-backup-crd -n cattle-resources-system --create-namespace --version $CHART_VERSION`, followed by `helm install rancher-backup rancher-charts/rancher-backup -n cattle-resources-system --version $CHART_VERSION`.

instruction: I've applied restore-migration.yaml on the target cluster. How do I check whether it's safe to move on to installing Rancher?
reference: Run `kubectl get restore` and wait until the Restore status is `Completed`. Then install cert-manager and Rancher (with the same hostname as before).

instruction: Moving our Rancher from an RKE2 local cluster to a K3s one. The restore is done; is there anything to adjust before installing Rancher there?
reference: Yes. Because the distribution changes, edit the local cluster object first with `kubectl edit clusters.management.cattle.io local`. Set `status.driver` to `imported`, remove `status.provider`, `status.version`, the `provider.cattle.io` label, the `management.cattle.io/current-cluster-controllers-version` annotation and `spec.rke2Config`, then save and install Rancher.

instruction: Cut-over to the new Rancher cluster is done and DNS points at it. What should we do on the old cluster so it doesn't interfere?
reference: Scale the original Rancher to zero replicas with `kubectl scale deployment rancher -n cattle-system --replicas=0` (using the old cluster's kubeconfig). This stops it from contacting managed clusters, which could otherwise leave them stuck in Updating.

instruction: Two downstream clusters are still disconnected an hour after our Rancher move, even though DNS is correct. What can I run on those clusters?
reference: Run `kubectl rollout restart deployment cattle-cluster-agent -n cattle-system` on each of them. The rolling restart makes the agent re-establish its connection to the new Rancher environment.
expect_command: kubectl rollout restart deployment cattle-cluster-agent -n cattle-system

instruction: I have an EKS-free, plain kubeadm cluster I want Rancher to manage. Walk me through bringing it in.
reference: In Rancher, go to ☰ > Cluster Management > Import Existing, choose the generic cluster type, set member roles and any agent environment variables, and click Create. Run the displayed `kubectl` command where kubeconfig points at the kubeadm cluster (check with `kubectl get nodes`). If Rancher uses a self-signed certificate, run the displayed `curl` command instead. The cluster starts as Pending and becomes Active.

instruction: I'm about to run Rancher's registration command on a cluster where my account only has namespace-level rights. What needs to happen first?
reference: Registration requires `cluster-admin` in that cluster. Have an admin grant it with `kubectl create clusterrolebinding cluster-admin-binding --clusterrole cluster-admin --user [USER_ACCOUNT]`, using your account, and then run the registration command.

instruction: After importing our cluster I see two projects I didn't create and a namespace list under one of them. Where did they come from?
reference: Rancher creates them automatically when a registered cluster becomes Active. The Default project holds the `default` namespace. The System project holds system namespaces such as `cattle-system`, `kube-public` and `kube-system`, if present.

instruction: We imported a production AKS cluster into Rancher as a test. If I remove it from Rancher now, will our workloads be affected?
reference: No. A registered (imported) AKS cluster is only disconnected when you delete it in Rancher. The cluster stays live and you can access it as before. Rancher only destroys EKS, AKS or GKE clusters that it created itself.

instruction: Rancher shows our new edge cluster as Pending for an hour. I have kubectl access to the edge cluster. What should I look at, and what command?
reference: Pending with `Waiting for full cluster configuration` means `cattle-cluster-agent` cannot connect to the Rancher `server-url`. On the edge cluster run `kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=cattle-cluster-agent -o wide` to check the agent pod is Running and not restarting, then read its logs.
expect_command: kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=cattle-cluster-agent -o wide

instruction: I suspect a TLS problem between a downstream cluster and Rancher. Which logs show the agent's connection attempts, and how do I fetch them?
reference: The cattle-cluster-agent logs show them. On the downstream cluster run `kubectl -n cattle-system logs -l app=cattle-cluster-agent`.

instruction: Our Kubernetes upgrade of a Rancher-provisioned RKE2 cluster isn't progressing on one node. Which Rancher component on the node carries out that kind of operation?
reference: `rancher-system-agent` does. It is the daemon Rancher uses on RKE2/K3s nodes to apply plans for lifecycle operations such as Kubernetes version upgrades and etcd snapshots. `cattle-cluster-agent` is the Deployment that connects to the cluster's Kubernetes API.

instruction: After a node reboot I'm not sure all three Rancher replicas came back. How do I see them and which nodes they landed on?
reference: Run `kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher -o wide`. The `-o wide` output shows the node for each pod. All replicas should be Running and `1/1` Ready.
expect_command: kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher -o wide

instruction: I want a GitOps repo to roll out a DaemonSet to every downstream cluster Rancher manages, but not to the Rancher server cluster itself. Which workspace should the GitRepo go in?
reference: Put it in `fleet-default`, which contains all downstream clusters registered through Rancher. `fleet-local` only contains the local cluster. Find it under ☰ > Continuous Delivery > Gitrepos.

instruction: Our repo mixes a Kustomize overlay and some bare manifests. Can SUSE Rancher Prime: Continuous Delivery handle that, and what does it actually use to apply them?
reference: Yes. Fleet (SUSE Rancher Prime: Continuous Delivery) handles raw YAML, Kustomize and Helm, or any combination. It dynamically turns all of them into Helm charts and uses Helm as the engine to deploy them.

instruction: My umbrella chart depends on a Redis subchart. When Fleet deploys it, the install errors about missing dependencies. What should be in my repo?
reference: The dependency charts must be committed under the chart's `charts/` subdirectory. Run `helm dependencies update $chart` (or `helm dependencies build $chart`) locally and commit the full `charts/` directory.

instruction: We migrated Rancher with the backup operator and everything came over except our private Git repos in Continuous Delivery, which now show auth errors. Expected?
reference: Yes, this is a documented known issue. Secrets referenced by Fleet GitRepos as `clientSecretName` and `helmSecretName` are not included in rancher-backup backups or restores. Recreate those secrets on the new cluster, or extend a ResourceSet to include them in future backups.

instruction: Security asked us to switch off every Rancher component we don't use; we don't use Continuous Delivery. What can actually be turned off there?
reference: Only the GitOps continuous delivery part. Set the `continuous-delivery` feature flag to false. The `gitjob` deployment is then no longer deployed in the local cluster and Continuous Delivery is hidden in the UI. Fleet itself comes preinstalled in Rancher and cannot be fully disabled.

instruction: Our dev team needs access to five namespaces in one cluster but nothing else. What's the Rancher-native way to set that up instead of five RoleBindings?
reference: Put the five namespaces in one Rancher project and add the team as project members with a project role. Permissions assigned at the project level are inherited by every namespace in that project, and members cannot access other projects in the cluster.

instruction: A developer with only project-owner rights ran `kubectl create ns feature-x` and now complains she gets forbidden errors in it. What should she do differently?
reference: Create namespaces through Rancher rather than kubectl. kubectl cannot scope a new namespace to her project, so the namespace is not in a project she has rights to. Creating it in Rancher, within her project, gives her access through the project's permissions.

instruction: After enabling Okta SAML, I noticed brand-new users can spin up clusters. Is that by design, and what controls it?
reference: Yes, by design. Users logging in through external authentication for the first time get the New User Default global permissions, which is Standard User by default, and Standard User includes creating clusters. Change the New User Default under ☰ > Users & Authentication > Role Templates, for example to User-Base or a custom role.

instruction: I need to give an auditor visibility into one team's project without letting them change anything. Which built-in role fits?
reference: Add the auditor as a member of that project with the Read Only project role. The built-in project roles are Owner, Member and Read Only, and non-admin users only see clusters and projects they have been explicitly added to.

instruction: I'm writing a bootstrap script that uses the Rancher CLI on a jump host. What's the non-interactive auth step, given I already have an API token?
reference: Log in with the token: `./rancher login https://<SERVER_URL> --token <BEARER_TOKEN>`, using your server URL and the bearer token from your API key. Then select the project with `./rancher context switch`.

instruction: I want to automate installing Rancher Logging on 30 clusters using only the `rancher` binary. Will that work?
reference: No. The Rancher CLI cannot install dashboard apps or Rancher feature charts such as Logging. Install them through Apps in the Rancher UI, or use another automation path such as Helm against each cluster.

instruction: Our CI system needs a token to call the Rancher API. Where do I generate it, and what should I keep in mind about storing it?
reference: Generate it from your user avatar > Account & API Keys > Create API Key, ideally with an expiration date and, if possible, a cluster scope. Store the bearer token (or access and secret key) securely right away, because Rancher shows it only once. Delete keys that expire or may be compromised.

instruction: Rancher is down for maintenance but I need to check nodes on our prod RKE2 cluster, which has ACE with an FQDN configured. How?
reference: Use the authorized cluster endpoint context from the downloaded kubeconfig: `kubectl --context <CLUSTER_NAME>-fqdn get nodes`. That context authenticates directly with the downstream cluster instead of going through Rancher.

instruction: Our internal ChartMuseum serves an index.yaml. How do I make its charts installable from the Rancher Apps page on a cluster?
reference: Explore that cluster, go to Apps > Repositories > Create, choose the http(s) URL to an index generated by Helm, and enter a name and the ChartMuseum index URL. After you create it, its charts appear on the Charts page under that repository name. Rancher re-syncs it every hour by default.

instruction: Before installing Monitoring on a small edge cluster, I want to know whether it will fit and what firewall rule is needed. What are the documented numbers?
reference: The cluster needs at least 1950Mi of memory, 2700m of CPU and 50Gi of storage available. Allow port 9796 on each node so Prometheus can scrape metrics. It installs from Cluster Tools into `cattle-monitoring-system`.

instruction: I'm designing the observability stack for a new SUSE Rancher Prime rollout. Should I standardise on the rancher-monitoring chart?
reference: Not for new installations. The current docs say `rancher-monitoring` is deprecated and no longer receives updates. It is kept only for existing deployments. Use the decoupled `rancher-monitoring-dashboards` chart instead.

instruction: A team lead wants to see and manage how their namespace's logs are shipped to Elasticsearch in Rancher. Which logging objects and roles are involved?
reference: Rancher Logging (built on the Logging operator) uses namespaced `Flows` and `Outputs`, plus cluster-wide `ClusterFlows` and `ClusterOutputs`, to route logs to destinations such as Elasticsearch. Access is controlled with the `logging-admin` and `logging-view` roles.

instruction: Our fluent pods from rancher-logging fail on nodes running lots of file watchers. Which kernel setting do I raise first, with the exact command?
reference: Raise the inotify limits. For instances, run `sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_instances=8192`. For watches, use `sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288`.

instruction: As part of DR planning, management asks: 'If we lose the Rancher server entirely, what happens to apps on the managed clusters, and can we still get in?' What's the answer?
reference: The workloads keep running. Registered clusters stay reachable the way they were before registration, and hosted clusters (EKS, AKS, GKE) through the provider's credentials. Rancher-provisioned RKE2/K3s clusters are reachable only if the authorized cluster endpoint was enabled and the kubeconfig was downloaded beforehand, so set that up in advance.

instruction: Our golden image is SLES and we want a single-node RKE2 control plane for a lab. Which installer invocation sets up the server?
reference: Use the RKE2 install script as root: `curl -sfL https://get.rke2.io | sh -`. It installs the rke2-server service and the rke2 binary; after that, enable and start rke2-server with systemctl.

instruction: After a maintenance window I find RKE2 didn't come back on a control-plane node because nobody had enabled it. How do I bring it up now and make it survive the next reboot?
reference: Enable and start the server unit: `systemctl enable rke2-server.service` so it starts on boot, then `systemctl start rke2-server.service` to bring it up now. Agents use rke2-agent.service.

instruction: We're adding six GPU workers to an existing RKE2 cluster. What do we run on each box to lay down the worker service?
reference: On each worker run the installer as an agent: `curl -sfL https://get.rke2.io | INSTALL_RKE2_TYPE="agent" sh -`. It installs rke2-agent; then point it at the cluster in /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml and start rke2-agent.service.

instruction: I'm writing cloud-init for RKE2 workers. Which two settings must the node's config file have, and what URL format does the server address take?
reference: The agent's /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml needs `server: https://<server>:9345` and `token: <token from server node>`. The URL uses the RKE2 supervisor port 9345, not 6443.

instruction: My colleague passes all RKE2 options as flags in a custom systemd drop-in. What's the documented primary way to configure RKE2 instead?
reference: The primary way is the config file at /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml, which you create manually. Its keys map directly to CLI flags, and you restart the RKE2 service after changing it.

instruction: I SSH'd into an RKE2 control-plane node to check pod status, but the shell has no kubectl and no kubeconfig in my home directory. Where do I find both?
reference: RKE2 puts kubectl in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin (not on PATH by default) and writes the admin kubeconfig to /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml. Run /var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin/kubectl with KUBECONFIG pointing to that file.

instruction: I installed upstream kubectl via my package manager on an RKE2 server and it tries localhost:8080. How do I make my session use RKE2's admin credentials?
reference: Point it at RKE2's kubeconfig: `export KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml`, then run kubectl as usual. You can also pass --kubeconfig /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml per command.

instruction: A teammate built the first RKE2 server without setting a token and has gone on leave. I need to join two more servers. Where can I recover the secret?
reference: Read it from the first server at /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/node-token, which RKE2 generates when no token was set, and use it as `token` on the joining servers.

instruction: After adding tls-san entries and restarting, our RKE2 control-plane node never becomes Ready. What do I run to stream its service output live?
reference: Stream the server unit's journal: `journalctl -u rke2-server -f`. On an agent you'd use journalctl -u rke2-agent -f.

instruction: We're putting an F5 virtual server in front of three RKE2 control-plane nodes. Which listener ports should the pool expose so both node joins and kubectl work?
reference: Expose TCP 9345 for RKE2 node registration (supervisor) and TCP 6443 for the Kubernetes API, both pointing to the server nodes.

instruction: Management wants to save money by running four RKE2 control-plane nodes instead of five, reasoning 'more than three is HA'. What does the RKE2 guidance say about the count?
reference: RKE2 calls for an odd number of server nodes, with three recommended, because etcd needs quorum. An even count like four adds a node without improving fault tolerance.

instruction: We templated server 1 with disable-kube-proxy: true for Cilium, but our Ansible role for servers 2 and 3 forgot it, and they won't come up. What's the likely cause?
reference: disable-kube-proxy is a critical value that must match on every RKE2 server. Mismatched servers fail with 'critical configuration value mismatch', so set the same value on servers 2 and 3.

instruction: Security review says application pods must never land on etcd/control-plane hosts in our RKE2 cluster. What setting achieves that?
reference: Set node-taint `CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoExecute` in the servers' config.yaml. RKE2 servers are schedulable by default, and this taint keeps user workloads off them.

instruction: Our template-built edge boxes all boot with the same hostname, and only one shows up in kubectl get nodes after joining RKE2. What are my options?
reference: RKE2 node names must be unique and default to the hostname. Give each box a unique hostname, set a unique node-name in config.yaml, or set with-node-id: true.

instruction: A pod on an RKE2 worker is stuck ContainerCreating and I want to inspect containers directly on the node with the CRI tool. What setup do I need?
reference: Run `export CRI_CONFIG_FILE=/var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/etc/crictl.yaml`, then use /var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin/crictl ps. RKE2's containerd socket is /run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock.

instruction: We're preparing RHEL 8.4 cloud images for RKE2. Which NetworkManager adjustments should be baked in before first boot?
reference: Add /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/rke2-canal.conf with a [keyfile] unmanaged-devices entry covering flannel*, cali*, tunl* and the Calico vxlan/wireguard interfaces. Also disable nm-cloud-setup.service and nm-cloud-setup.timer.

instruction: We're decommissioning a tarball-installed RKE2 worker and want it clean before reimaging. What script do we run?
reference: Run `/usr/local/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh`. It stops RKE2, removes the binary and cleans up its files. RPM installs use /usr/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh instead.

instruction: An architect asks how RKE2 runs the API server and scheduler compared with RKE1. What's the answer?
reference: RKE2 runs control plane components as static pods managed by the kubelet, with embedded containerd. RKE1 used Docker for this, and RKE2 does not rely on Docker.

instruction: An auditor asks what our RKE2 cluster's out-of-the-box etcd backup schedule and local retention are, assuming we've configured nothing. What do I tell them?
reference: By default RKE2 takes scheduled etcd snapshots at 00:00 and 12:00 system time (cron 0 */12 * * *) and keeps 5 per server node under /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/snapshots.

instruction: Change control requires a fresh etcd backup immediately before we rotate certificates on our RKE2 control plane. What do I execute on a server?
reference: Take an on-demand snapshot with `rke2 etcd-snapshot save` on a server node. It is saved as on-demand-<node>-<timestamp> and is not pruned automatically.

instruction: Our monitoring runs off-cluster with only API access. How can it check that recent etcd snapshots exist on each of the three RKE2 servers?
reference: Query ETCDSnapshotFile resources through the API: `kubectl get etcdsnapshotfile`. They track snapshots on all members, while rke2 etcd-snapshot list only sees the local node.

instruction: Our pre-deploy pipeline calls rke2 etcd-snapshot save every release, and /var is now 90% full. What housekeeping command should the pipeline add?
reference: Add a prune step: `rke2 etcd-snapshot prune --snapshot-retention <NUM-OF-SNAPSHOTS-TO-RETAIN>`. On-demand snapshots have no automatic retention, so this flag is required.

instruction: A bad Helm upgrade corrupted CRDs on our one-node RKE2 lab. I have /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/snapshots/etcd-snapshot-lab-1700000000. Walk me through getting back to it.
reference: Stop RKE2 (`systemctl stop rke2-server`), then run `rke2 server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=<PATH-TO-SNAPSHOT>` with that file as the path. When it says to restart without --cluster-reset, run `systemctl start rke2-server`.

instruction: We did a cluster-reset restore on cp-1 of our RKE2 trio. cp-2 and cp-3 are still stopped. What has to happen on those two before they start?
reference: Remove their old etcd data with `rm -rf /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/` (backing it up first if needed), then start rke2-server so they rejoin the restored cluster.

instruction: Our DR runbook rebuilds the RKE2 control plane in another datacenter from S3 snapshots. Which secret from the old cluster must the runbook also preserve, and why?
reference: Preserve the server token from /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/token and pass it with --token during the restore. It is needed to decrypt the bootstrap data inside the snapshot.

instruction: We store RKE2 S3 credentials in a kube-system Secret via etcd-s3-config-secret. During a DR restore from S3, will RKE2 pick the credentials from that Secret?
reference: No. The S3 config Secret can't be used during a restore because the apiserver isn't running. Pass the S3 settings (--etcd-s3, --etcd-s3-bucket and so on) on the CLI with --cluster-reset.

instruction: We have 3 RKE2 servers and 40 workers on v1.32 and need to reach v1.34 this quarter. How should the rollout be sequenced?
reference: Go one minor at a time (v1.33, then v1.34) because of the Kubernetes version skew policy. At each step, upgrade the servers first, one at a time, and then the agents.

instruction: Our change ticket says to move this RKE2 control-plane node to an exact approved release using the official script. What do I run, and what's the follow-up step?
reference: Run `curl -sfL https://get.rke2.io | INSTALL_RKE2_VERSION=vX.Y.Z+rke2rN sh -` with the approved tag, then `systemctl restart rke2-server`. On agents, add INSTALL_RKE2_TYPE=agent and restart rke2-agent.

instruction: We run a standalone RKE2 cluster (not managed by Rancher) and want Kubernetes-native, declarative upgrades. What's the first component to install and how?
reference: Install Rancher's system-upgrade-controller with `kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rancher/system-upgrade-controller/releases/latest/download/crd.yaml -f https://github.com/rancher/system-upgrade-controller/releases/latest/download/system-upgrade-controller.yaml`, then define server and agent Plans using rancher/rke2-upgrade.

instruction: Ops wants to apply a server-plan YAML to an RKE2 cluster that shows up in our Rancher Prime dashboard as 'Imported'. Any concern?
reference: Yes. For imported RKE2 clusters, Rancher manages the system-upgrade-controller and plans by default. Upgrade through Rancher unless version management has been disabled for that cluster.

instruction: We're planning a new RKE2 cluster that will include Windows workers. Which of the bundled CNIs can we pick, and where is that choice made?
reference: Only Calico and Flannel support Windows among RKE2's bundled CNIs (Canal is the default). Set it with the cni key in /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml before the first start.

instruction: I need jumbo frames (MTU 9000) for Calico on a new RKE2 GPU cluster. Where and how do I express that override?
reference: Add a HelmChartConfig named rke2-calico in kube-system, with valuesContent setting installation.calicoNetwork.mtu: 9000. Put it in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests (for example rke2-calico-config.yaml).

instruction: I'm writing a runbook for a brand-new RKE2 v1.36 cluster. Out of the box, which ingress controller will it run, and how could I make that explicit in config?
reference: New RKE2 clusters from v1.36 default to Traefik (earlier versions used ingress-nginx). Make it explicit with ingress-controller: traefik in config.yaml.

instruction: Our Harbor instance needs basic auth and a custom CA. Which file on RKE2 nodes carries those settings, and which section holds the credentials?
reference: Use /etc/rancher/rke2/registries.yaml on each node. Under configs, add the registry with auth (username/password) and tls (ca_file), then restart RKE2.

instruction: Image pulls through our Nexus pull-through cache intermittently fail on one RKE2 worker, and the event only says 'dial tcp: lookup registry-1.docker.io'. Where should I look for the actual mirror error?
reference: Check /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/containerd/containerd.log on that worker. The kubelet event only shows the final attempt against the default endpoint, which containerd tries last.

instruction: A submarine-deployed RKE2 box will never see a network or registry. Where on disk should the image bundle go so RKE2 can bring up its system pods?
reference: Copy the release's images archive (for example rke2-images.linux-amd64.tar.zst) into /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/images/ before starting RKE2. It imports archives from there at startup.

instruction: We've carried a USB stick with the RKE2 tarball, images archive, checksum file and install.sh into a disconnected lab, copied to /root/rke2-artifacts. How do we install so the systemd units are created?
reference: Run the script against that directory: `INSTALL_RKE2_ARTIFACT_PATH=/root/rke2-artifacts sh install.sh`. It runs a normal install, including the systemd units, using the local artifacts.

instruction: Our classified enclave nodes have only a /24 with no gateway configured. After installing RKE2, kubectl get nodes -o wide shows odd INTERNAL-IP values. What prerequisite is probably missing?
reference: A default route. RKE2 needs one to auto-detect the node's primary IP and for ClusterIP routing. Add one (a dummy-interface black-hole route works) before RKE2 starts.

instruction: I'm hardening a new tarball-installed RKE2 host before first start. What exact copy step puts RKE2's CIS kernel settings in place?
reference: Run `sudo cp -f /usr/local/share/rke2/rke2-cis-sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/60-rke2-cis.conf`, then sudo systemctl restart systemd-sysctl. RPM installs use /usr/share/rke2/rke2-cis-sysctl.conf.

instruction: CIS control 1.1.12 wants the etcd data directory owned by etcd:etcd on our RKE2 servers. What host prep satisfies that?
reference: Create a local etcd user and group with `sudo useradd -r -c "etcd user" -s /sbin/nologin -M etcd -U` before starting RKE2 with the CIS profile. RKE2 then creates the etcd data directory owned by etcd and runs etcd as that user.

instruction: Our compliance team wants the RKE2 v1.33 cluster to pass the CIS benchmark with minimal manual tuning. Which single config setting do we add, and what pod security behaviour should app teams expect?
reference: Add profile: "cis" to /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml. App teams should expect Pod Security Admission restricted mode in every namespace except kube-system, compliance-operator-system and tigera-operator.

instruction: I want a NetworkPolicy and a namespace created automatically every time our RKE2 control plane boots, without running kubectl by hand. Where do I drop the YAML?
reference: Put it in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests on the server nodes. RKE2 applies files there like kubectl apply at startup and when they change. Keep the files in sync across servers yourself.

instruction: A developer wants a throwaway Kubernetes on an Alpine VM that uses openrc. Which official command sets K3s up as a service?
reference: Use the K3s install script, which supports systemd and openrc: `curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -`. It sets up the service, bundled kubectl and the kubeconfig at /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml.

instruction: I have a K3s server at 192.168.1.10 and want to attach an old laptop as compute. What's the documented install form for the laptop?
reference: Use the agent form of the installer: `curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://myserver:6443 K3S_TOKEN=mynodetoken sh -`, with https://192.168.1.10:6443 as K3S_URL and the token from /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token as K3S_TOKEN.

instruction: I'm moving a K3s node's settings out of install-script flags into a file. What path does K3s read, and where will the admin kubeconfig remain?
reference: Put settings in /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml (drop-ins in /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml.d/). The admin kubeconfig stays at /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml.

instruction: Our K3s fleet was installed with long INSTALL_K3S_EXEC strings, and every upgrade someone forgets a flag. What's the documented way to stop that drift?
reference: Move the settings into /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml. Install-script options are lost if not repeated on re-run, but the script doesn't manage the config file.

instruction: We're building a three-node K3s control plane at a retail site with no external database. What do I run on the very first node?
reference: Initialize embedded etcd on the first server: `curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_TOKEN=SECRET sh -s - server --cluster-init`. The other two then join with the same token and --server https://<server1>:6443.

instruction: Our K3s dev box has been running for a year with default settings, and now we want two more control-plane nodes. What's the migration step on the existing server?
reference: It uses embedded SQLite by default, which can't serve multiple servers. Restart that K3s server with --cluster-init to convert it to embedded etcd, then join the new servers.

instruction: We're writing security-group rules for a K3s cluster on Flannel VXLAN with three embedded-etcd servers. What inbound rules do we need?
reference: Allow TCP 6443 to servers (supervisor and API) and UDP 8472 between all nodes for VXLAN. Add TCP 10250 between nodes for kubelet metrics and TCP 2379-2380 between servers for etcd.

instruction: Before I let an intern experiment with CRDs on our embedded-etcd K3s cluster, I'd like an immediate backup. What do I run?
reference: Take an on-demand snapshot on a server: `k3s etcd-snapshot save`. It's stored under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/snapshots and is not auto-pruned.

instruction: Our K3s home lab's etcd got wedged after a power cut. I have last night's snapshot file on the server. What's the recovery sequence?
reference: Stop K3s (`systemctl stop k3s`), run `k3s server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=<PATH-TO-SNAPSHOT>` with the snapshot file, then `systemctl start k3s` after it says to restart without --cluster-reset.

instruction: We want K3s at the edge but our network team mandates Cilium. What startup options should the K3s servers use?
reference: Start the servers with --flannel-backend=none so Flannel isn't deployed, and --disable-network-policy to avoid conflicts. Then install Cilium.

instruction: We're standardizing on ingress-nginx across all our K3s clusters. How do we stop K3s shipping its default ingress controller?
reference: K3s deploys Traefik by default. Start the servers with --disable=traefik (or disable: traefik in config.yaml), which also uninstalls it from existing clusters.

instruction: Factory-floor K3s nodes have no outbound internet. I've copied the binary to /usr/local/bin and the images tarball into place. How do I run the installer so it creates the service without fetching anything?
reference: Run the local script with downloads skipped: `INSTALL_K3S_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true ./install.sh`. It uses the binary already in /usr/local/bin and creates the service.

instruction: Our K3s edge sites pull through a regional Zot cache. Which file on each node should contain the mirror definition?
reference: Put the mirror under mirrors in /etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml on each node that pulls images, then restart K3s.

instruction: Security wants all K3s nodes on a particular patched release by Friday. What does the install-script based upgrade look like for a node?
reference: Re-run the installer with the target version and the node's original settings: `curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=vX.Y.Z+k3s1 <EXISTING_K3S_ENV> sh -s - <EXISTING_K3S_ARGS>`. It downloads the binary and restarts K3s. Do servers one at a time, then agents.

instruction: We're retiring a single-node K3s test server and want everything K3s created on it gone. What do we run?
reference: Run `/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh` on the server. It removes K3s, the local datastore, local-storage volume data, node configuration and the bundled tools. Agents use k3s-agent-uninstall.sh.

instruction: A customer's change-management form asks for the namespace their SUSE Storage pods will run in. What should they write?
reference: They should write longhorn-system. SUSE Storage is derived from upstream Longhorn and keeps the longhorn nomenclature for its Kubernetes resources, so its components run in the longhorn-system namespace and its custom resources use the longhorn.io API group.

instruction: An architect asks which SUSE Storage component is the control plane and which is the data plane. How do you answer?
reference: The Longhorn Manager is the control plane; it runs on every node as a Kubernetes DaemonSet and creates and manages volumes. The Longhorn Engine is the data plane; SUSE Storage creates a dedicated engine (storage controller) for each volume.

instruction: A performance engineer wants to know where the I/O path starts for a SUSE Storage RWO volume and how writes reach the replicas. What is the answer?
reference: The I/O path starts at the Longhorn Engine, which always runs on the same node as the pod using the volume. The engine synchronously replicates each write to the volume's replicas, which are stored on multiple nodes.

instruction: Volume I/O is slow only on worker3. Which SUSE Storage pod should I inspect on that node, and how do I identify it?
reference: Inspect the Instance Manager pod on worker3, because it hosts the engine and replica instances for the volumes on that node; there is no separate per-volume engine pod. Instance Manager pods are named instance-manager-<hash> in longhorn-system and carry the longhorn.io/node=<node-name> label, so you can select the one for worker3 and use kubectl logs or kubectl exec on it.

instruction: A customer runs single-replica volumes to save disk. How many replica failures can those volumes tolerate in SUSE Storage?
reference: None. A volume with N replicas tolerates at most N-1 replica failures, so with N=1 it tolerates zero; losing that replica leaves no healthy replica for the volume to stay operational.

instruction: Capacity planning: our app writes 50 GB of temp files daily and deletes them. Will the SUSE Storage volume's on-disk usage drop after each deletion?
reference: Not by itself. SUSE Storage thin-provisions volumes, but it operates at the block level and cannot tell that the file system deleted content, so the actual size on disk does not shrink after deletions. Plan for the high-water mark, or reclaim space with a filesystem trim.

instruction: An auditor asks whether SUSE Storage snapshots count as off-site copies. What do you tell them?
reference: They do not. SUSE Storage snapshots are stored locally as part of each replica on the cluster nodes' disks. Off-cluster copies are backups, which are written to an external backupstore (NFS or S3-compatible) and remain retrievable if the cluster is unavailable.

instruction: We're estimating backup bandwidth for a database volume that makes many small random writes. What about SUSE Storage's backup granularity should we account for?
reference: Account for the 2 MB backup block size. SUSE Storage backups are incremental, but they upload changed data in 2 MB blocks, so a single changed 4K block causes its whole 2 MB block to be backed up. Many scattered small writes can therefore produce more backup traffic than the raw bytes written.

instruction: I'm templating a Helm chart that creates a StorageClass for SUSE Storage volumes. Which value goes in the provisioner field?
reference: Set `provisioner: driver.longhorn.io`. For SUSE Storage the StorageClass provisioner is always driver.longhorn.io, the Longhorn CSI driver.

instruction: I need a StorageClass for scratch data that keeps the SUSE Storage default redundancy explicit. What exact parameter line do I write?
reference: Write `numberOfReplicas: "3"` under parameters. numberOfReplicas defaults to 3 and accepts values from 1 to 20.

instruction: For a hyper-converged setup we want 2 replicas, one ideally on the pod's node, but the volume must not fail if that's impossible. Which dataLocality line fits?
reference: Use `dataLocality: "best-effort"` together with numberOfReplicas: "2". best-effort keeps a replica on the workload's node when possible without stopping the volume if it cannot; strict-local would not fit because it requires a single replica.

instruction: After a review we raised numberOfReplicas from 2 to 3 in our production StorageClass. Will the 40 existing PVCs now get a third replica?
reference: No. SUSE Storage applies StorageClass parameters only when a volume is created, and modifying the StorageClass does not propagate to existing volumes. Only new PVCs get 3 replicas; the existing volumes must be updated individually.

instruction: Our NVMe disks are tagged ssd and fast in SUSE Storage. I want a 'gold' StorageClass whose replicas land only on those disks. What do I add?
reference: Add `diskSelector: "ssd,fast"` under the StorageClass parameters. diskSelector restricts replica placement to disks carrying the listed storage tags, and with multiple tags a disk must have all of them.

instruction: We're benchmarking SPDK-based volumes. What do I set in our test StorageClass so PVCs use the V2 Data Engine?
reference: Set `dataEngine: "v2"` in the StorageClass parameters (the default is "v1"). The V2 Data Engine must be enabled and block-type disks must exist, because V2 volumes are scheduled only to block-type disks.

instruction: A team wants a shared upload directory for 6 web pods across nodes, on SUSE Storage. What component will serve it, and what node prerequisite matters?
reference: Use an RWX PVC. SUSE Storage serves it from a share-manager-<volume-name> pod in longhorn-system that runs an NFSv4.1 server in front of a regular Longhorn volume. Every node that runs one of the web pods needs an NFSv4 client installed.

instruction: I'm writing a cloud-init snippet for new SLES worker nodes so they can mount SUSE Storage ReadWriteMany volumes. Which package install line do I include?
reference: Include `zypper install nfs-client`. RWX volumes are served over NFSv4.1, so every SUSE or openSUSE node that mounts them needs the NFSv4 client.

instruction: Our NFS clients need NFS 4.2 for a shared RWX volume on SUSE Storage, but we want to keep the default failure semantics. What parameter line goes in the StorageClass, and what's the catch?
reference: Use `nfsOptions: "vers=4.2,noresvport,softerr,timeo=600,retrans=5"`. The catch is that nfsOptions replaces the defaults entirely, so you must list the complete set of options, and SUSE Storage does not validate the string; an invalid value makes the mount fail.

instruction: A virtualization team plans to live-migrate VMs between nodes using SUSE Storage disks. What three conditions must their PVCs and StorageClass meet?
reference: They need migratable RWX volumes: the StorageClass must set migratable: "true", and the PVCs must use the ReadWriteMany access mode with volumeMode: Block. Filesystem mode is not supported for migratable volumes.

instruction: A data science team wants 10 pods to read the same reference dataset but never write to it. Which access mode should they request on SUSE Storage?
reference: Request ReadWriteMany and mount the volume read-only in the pod specifications. SUSE Storage does not support ReadOnlyMany (ROX); the documented approach for multi-pod read-only access is RWX with read-only mount options.

instruction: I'm building a SUSE-based golden image for RKE2 workers that will run V1 SUSE Storage volumes. Which iSCSI-related commands belong in the image build?
reference: Include `zypper install open-iscsi`, then `systemctl enable iscsid` and `systemctl start iscsid`. V1 volumes use iSCSI, so each node needs open-iscsi with the iscsid service running.

instruction: Our repo mirror just synced open-iscsi 2.1.12 and the patch window is tonight. Should SUSE Storage nodes take it?
reference: No. Hold that package back. open-iscsi 2.1.12 has a breaking configuration change that causes SUSE Storage volume attachment failures; stay on 2.1.11 or earlier, or wait for 2.1.13 or later.

instruction: Our minimal SLES image uses kernel-default-base and Longhorn V1 volumes fail to attach. What's the likely cause and the check?
reference: The likely cause is a missing iscsi_tcp module: on SUSE and openSUSE it ships only in kernel-default, not kernel-default-base. Switch to kernel-default and confirm the module loads with `modprobe iscsi_tcp` before iscsid starts.

instruction: Three new workers joined the cluster. Without touching them by SSH, how can I verify they are ready for SUSE Storage V1 volumes?
reference: Use the Longhorn CLI: run `./longhornctl check preflight`. It checks each node for items such as a running iscsid service, NFS4 support and installed open-iscsi and NFS packages, and longhornctl install preflight can install anything missing.

instruction: We're specifying hardware for nodes that will run SUSE Storage V2 volumes. What CPU, memory and disk requirements go on the purchase spec?
reference: Specify AMD64 CPUs with SSE4.2 (or ARM64), 2 GiB of RAM per node reserved as 2 MiB huge pages (1024 pages), and raw block disks for V2 volumes, ideally local NVMe. Also plan the OS for kernel 6.7 or later with the vfio_pci, uio_pci_generic and nvme-tcp modules.

instruction: On a test VM I need SPDK's huge pages available immediately for a quick SUSE Storage V2 experiment. What's the one-liner, and what's its limitation?
reference: Run `echo 1024 > /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages` to allocate 1024 2 MiB pages (2 GiB). The limitation is that it is not persistent across reboots; for persistence use the hugepagesz=2M hugepages=1024 kernel boot parameters.

instruction: I've prepared hugepages and kernel modules on all nodes. What's the next step to actually activate V2 in SUSE Storage, and what should I expect?
reference: Set the v2-data-engine setting to true (Settings > V2 Data Engine in the UI). The instance-manager pods restart automatically, and the change is blocked while volumes are attached, so detach volumes first. Then add block-type disks to the nodes for V2 volumes.

instruction: A platform team wants to keep V1 for most apps and turn on V2 'just in case' on the same production cluster. What does SUSE recommend?
reference: SUSE recommends enabling only one data engine per cluster. Running both means every node runs separate V1 and V2 instance-manager pods with separate CPU reservations, and the V2 instance-manager typically takes a dedicated CPU core for spdk_tgt polling, so the 'just in case' setup costs CPU on every node.

instruction: We attached a new 2 TB NVMe to each node and want SUSE Storage V1 volumes to use it. Do we add it raw or formatted?
reference: Formatted. V1 volumes are scheduled only to filesystem-type disks, so format the NVMe with an extent-based file system such as ext4 or XFS, mount it on the host and add the mount path. Raw block-type disks are only used by V2 volumes.

instruction: Management wants to know the maturity of SUSE Storage V2 in version 1.12, including the new erasure-coding option, before approving it. Summarize.
reference: The V2 Data Engine is generally available as of SUSE Storage v1.12.0 and is described as suitable for production in supported environments. Storage sharding with erasure coding, added in v1.12.1, is experimental and not recommended for production, so approve V2 with the default replicated layout only.

instruction: A latency-sensitive app currently uses V1 volumes with dataLocality strict-local. The team wants the V2 engine for performance. What constraint do they hit?
reference: strict-local data locality is not supported on the V2 Data Engine; V2 supports only disabled and best-effort. They must either stay on V1 to keep strict-local or accept best-effort locality on V2.

instruction: An old edge cluster still runs SUSE Storage 1.9.2 and the team wants to land on 1.12.1 in a single maintenance window. Is that possible?
reference: Not in a single jump. SUSE Storage only supports upgrading to the next consecutive minor version, and skipping minor versions fails automatically, so the path is 1.9.x to 1.10.x to 1.11.x to 1.12.1. Downgrades are not supported, so back up before each step.

instruction: Change ticket: move our Helm-managed SUSE Storage from 1.11.4 to 1.12.1. What command should the ticket list?
reference: List `helm upgrade longhorn oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/suse-storage --namespace longhorn-system --version <version> --set global.imagePullSecrets=<PULL_IMAGE_SECRET>` with <version> set to 1.12.1 and your pull secret, plus -f values.yaml if you use custom values. 1.11.x to 1.12 is a supported consecutive minor upgrade.

instruction: Write a short pre-upgrade checklist for our SUSE Storage maintenance window. We run a mix of V1 and V2 volumes.
reference: 1) Detach all V2 Data Engine volumes and confirm their replicas are stopped, since V2 has no live upgrade. 2) Confirm no volume is Faulted and no BackingImage is failed. 3) Back up volumes and create a Longhorn system backup. 4) Verify the target is the next consecutive minor version.

instruction: We upgraded the SUSE Storage chart, but nobody wants to click through 300 volumes to upgrade engines. What setting handles this and what value is advised?
reference: Set Concurrent Automatic Engine Upgrade Per Node Limit to a value above 0; SUSE Storage recommends 3. With the default of 0 no automatic engine upgrade happens; with it set, attached healthy volumes get a live engine upgrade and detached volumes an offline upgrade.
expect_any: Concurrent Automatic Engine Upgrade Per Node Limit

instruction: The Helm install of SUSE Storage returned successfully. What do I run to confirm the components are actually up?
reference: Run `kubectl -n longhorn-system get pod` and confirm longhorn-manager, longhorn-ui, longhorn-driver-deployer, longhorn-csi-plugin, the csi-* pods, instance-manager and engine-image pods are Running.

instruction: Our S3 bucket is 'lh-prod' in eu-central-1 and we want backups under a 'cluster-a' prefix. What URL should the SUSE Storage backup target use?
reference: Use s3://lh-prod@eu-central-1/cluster-a/. The documented form is `s3://<your-bucket-name>@<your-aws-region>/`; the region is required, the URL must end with a slash, and a subdirectory prefix may be appended.

instruction: Security gave us an IAM user's access key pair for Longhorn backups. What's the exact command to store it so SUSE Storage can use it?
reference: Run `kubectl create secret generic <aws-secret> --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<your-aws-access-key-id> --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<your-aws-secret-access-key> -n longhorn-system`, then select that secret as the backup target's Credential Secret. It must be in longhorn-system.

instruction: We have an NFSv4 export at nfs-backup.storage.svc:/exports/lh. How should the SUSE Storage backup target be written, and what mount options will apply?
reference: Write it as nfs://nfs-backup.storage.svc:/exports/lh, following the documented form `nfs://longhorn-test-nfs-svc.default:/opt/backupstore`. With no nfsOptions, SUSE Storage uses actimeo=1,soft,timeo=300,retry=2; custom options go in an nfsOptions query parameter.

instruction: Compliance requires that backups older than 30 days disappear. A colleague proposes an S3 bucket expiration rule on the SUSE Storage bucket. Your advice?
reference: Do not use a bucket expiration rule. SUSE Storage manages the backup lifecycle in the backupstore entirely, and applying retention policies directly on it is prohibited. Size the retain count of the recurring backup job to match 30 days of backups instead.

instruction: I want nightly backups at 02:00 keeping 14 copies, applied automatically to all volumes without their own schedule. What should the RecurringJob look like conceptually?
reference: Create a RecurringJob in longhorn-system with task: backup, cron: "0 2 * * *", retain: 14, a concurrency of at least 1, and groups including default. Jobs in the default group are applied to every volume that has no recurring job.

instruction: A single critical volume needs the extra 'hourly-snap' recurring job on top of the defaults. Which kubectl command assigns it?
reference: Use `kubectl -n longhorn-system label volume/<VOLUME-NAME> recurring-job.longhorn.io/<RECURRING-JOB-NAME>=enabled` with hourly-snap as the job name, i.e. the label recurring-job.longhorn.io/hourly-snap=enabled on that Longhorn volume.

instruction: App teams only have RBAC on PVCs in their namespaces, not on Longhorn volumes. How can they still opt their data into recurring backups?
reference: Have them label the PVC as the source first with `kubectl -n <NAMESPACE> label pvc/<PVC-NAME> recurring-job.longhorn.io/source=enabled`, then add recurring job labels such as recurring-job.longhorn.io/backup=enabled on the PVC. SUSE Storage periodically syncs those labels to the volume.

instruction: We want every PVC from the 'longhorn-db' StorageClass to get the 'backup' recurring job group without extra labeling. What parameter do we add?
reference: Add `recurringJobSelector: '[{"name":"backup", "isGroup":true}]'` to the StorageClass parameters. The group must already exist, and volumes created from the class afterwards get it assigned automatically.

instruction: We need a warm standby of our primary cluster's database volume in a second region using SUSE Storage. What's the mechanism and what drives the recovery point?
reference: Use a disaster recovery volume in the second cluster. Both clusters point at the same backup target; the DR volume is created from a backup of the source volume and polls for and incrementally restores newer backups. Replication is asynchronous through backups, so the recurring backup frequency on the source volume determines the potential data loss.

instruction: During DR drills, half our DR volumes activate fine and the rest hang in 'Attached' forever. The hanging ones show failed replicas. What setting do we check?
reference: Check Allow Volume Creation with Degraded Availability. Degraded DR volumes, those with failed replicas, can only be activated when that setting is enabled; otherwise activation leaves them stuck in the Attached state. Once enabled, they activate and become normal Detached volumes.
expect_any: Allow Volume Creation with Degraded Availability

instruction: I need a VolumeSnapshotClass so that `kubectl apply` of a VolumeSnapshot sends data to our S3 backupstore via SUSE Storage. What's the key parameter?
reference: Set `type: bak` in the VolumeSnapshotClass parameters, with driver: driver.longhorn.io. VolumeSnapshots using that class create Longhorn backups in the backup target, referenced as bak://backup-volume/backup-name.

instruction: A bad migration script corrupted tables an hour ago; we have a Longhorn snapshot from before it ran. Outline how to roll the volume back safely.
reference: Stop the workload so the volume is detached, then attach it from the UI with maintenance mode enabled, which attaches it without the frontend so nothing can access the data, and revert to the pre-migration snapshot. Then detach and let the workload reattach it normally.

instruction: I've mounted a new XFS disk at /mnt/data2 on node worker5. Without the UI, how do I hand it to SUSE Storage for V1 volumes?
reference: Run `kubectl edit node.longhorn.io <node-name>` for worker5 and add a disk under spec.disks with path: /mnt/data2, diskType: filesystem and allowScheduling: true. Make sure the mount is in /etc/fstab so it persists after reboot.

instruction: We're recycling NVMe drives from an old ext4 setup for SUSE Storage V2. What must we run on each drive before adding it, and why?
reference: Run `wipefs -a /path/to/block/device` on each drive. SUSE Storage refuses to add block-type disks that still carry a file system or partition table, so the old ext4 signatures must be removed first.

instruction: We moved SUSE Storage to dedicated 4 TB data disks. Which scheduling-headroom setting can we tune, and to what?
reference: Lower Storage Minimal Available Percentage from its default of 25 to 10, which the best practices allow for dedicated disks. Tune Storage Over Provisioning Percentage (default 100) based on how full volumes typically get, for example 200 if they use about half their size.

instruction: I only have SSH and kubectl access to the cluster, no UI. How do I change the SUSE Storage setting replica-replenishment-wait-interval?
reference: Run `kubectl edit settings.longhorn.io <SETTING-NAME> -n longhorn-system` with replica-replenishment-wait-interval as the setting name, and edit its value. Use settings.longhorn.io or lhs rather than plain settings to avoid CRD name collisions.

instruction: Our automated OS patching pipeline gets stuck draining storage nodes, and the stuck node always has a single-replica volume on it. What SUSE Storage behavior explains this?
reference: The default Node Drain Policy, block-if-contains-last-replica, blocks the drain while the node holds the last healthy replica of a volume, and a single-replica volume always has its last replica there. For automation with numberOfReplicas 1, the docs point to block-for-eviction or block-for-eviction-if-contains-last-replica during planned maintenance, which evict replicas automatically.

instruction: In a node-failure test, our Deployment's replacement pod waited forever for its Longhorn RWO volume. Which setting changes this, and what's its default?
reference: Pod Deletion Policy When Node is Down. Its default is do-nothing, so the terminating pod on the failed node is never force-deleted and the RWO volume stays attached. Setting it to delete-deployment-pod (or delete-both-statefulset-and-deployment-pod) lets SUSE Storage force-delete the pod so the volume is released.
expect_any: Pod Deletion Policy When Node is Down

instruction: Support asked for 'the Longhorn diagnostics' for a volume attach failure. What exactly should I send, and is anything missing from it?
reference: Send a support bundle generated with the Generate Support Bundle link at the bottom of the SUSE Storage UI; it is a zip with SUSE Storage-related configuration and logs. It does not include dmesg, so collect dmesg from the affected nodes separately.

instruction: After adding autoscaled nodes from a minimal image, pods with an RWX SUSE Storage volume fail with a mount helper program error on those nodes only. What's the fix?
reference: Install an NFSv4 client in the node image. SUSE Storage RWX volumes are mounted over NFS, and a missing client produces the '/sbin/mount.<type> helper program' mount error.

instruction: A small edge site has exactly two worker nodes with disks for SUSE Storage. What replica count should we standardize on there?
reference: Standardize on 2 replicas. SUSE Storage recommends 3 when there are three or more storage nodes and 2 otherwise; set numberOfReplicas: "2" in the StorageClass and the Default Replica Count for UI-created volumes.

instruction: We're decommissioning a lab cluster and want SUSE Storage gone cleanly. What setting must be flipped first, and which command removes it?
reference: Set deleting-confirmation-flag to true, otherwise the uninstallation job fails, and remove workloads using SUSE Storage volumes. Then run `helm uninstall longhorn -n longhorn-system`.

instruction: Every new GPU node we add has two NVMe mounts, /mnt/disk1 and /mnt/disk2. How do we make SUSE Storage set up both disks automatically at join time?
reference: Enable Create Default Disk on Labeled Nodes, label the nodes with `node.longhorn.io/create-default-disk: 'config'`, and annotate them with node.longhorn.io/default-disks-config containing a JSON list with entries for /mnt/disk1 and /mnt/disk2. It applies only to nodes without existing disks or tags.

instruction: On a single-node test cluster, every new volume reports 2 of 3 replicas unscheduled. Which setting explains this?
reference: Replica Node Level Soft Anti-Affinity, which defaults to false. With it disabled, SUSE Storage will not schedule another replica on a node that already has a healthy replica of the volume, so one node can host only one. Use one replica on a single-node cluster, or enable the setting.

instruction: A brief top-of-rack switch outage made every replica of several volumes fault at once. Will SUSE Storage bring those volumes back by itself, and which setting governs it?
reference: Yes, as long as Automatic Salvage is enabled, which it is by default. When all replicas become faulty, for example after a network disconnection, SUSE Storage identifies the usable replicas and uses them for the volume.

instruction: My manager asked what open-source pieces sit inside SUSE Virtualization. Which ones should I list?
reference: List Kubernetes as the base, KubeVirt for virtualization management with KVM, SUSE Storage (Longhorn) for distributed block storage, an immutable SUSE Linux Micro based operating system, and Grafana with Prometheus for observability. SUSE Virtualization is the product name; Harvester is the project name.

instruction: I'm checking compatibility for a 1.8.x cluster. What OS release and RKE2 minor do the nodes run?
reference: SUSE Virtualization v1.8.x nodes run SUSE Linux Micro 6.2 and RKE2 v1.35. The same release uses KubeVirt v1.7, SUSE Storage (Longhorn) v1.11 and SUSE Rancher Prime v2.14.

instruction: A candidate server has 16 cores, 64 GB RAM, a single 400 GB SSD and 10 GbE. Does it meet the SUSE Virtualization production minimums?
reference: Not quite. The 16 cores, 64 GB of memory and 10 Gbps Ethernet meet the production minimums, but the disk does not: production nodes need at least 500 GB, with 1 TB or more recommended. 400 GB only meets the development/testing minimum of 250 GB.

instruction: A colleague wants to reuse some old SATA spinning drives for a new SUSE Virtualization cluster's management nodes. What do the requirements say about disk type and speed?
reference: The requirements call for 5,000+ random IOPS per disk, meaning SSD or NVMe, and management node storage must meet etcd speed requirements. Only local disks and hardware RAID are supported, so slow spinning drives do not meet the requirement.

instruction: I'd like to test SUSE Virtualization 1.8 by installing it inside a VM on my laptop, booting with BIOS. Will that work?
reference: That setup is not supported. From v1.8.0, new installations are only possible on UEFI systems, and the requirements state that laptops and nested virtualization are not supported. Use bare-metal UEFI servers, all with the same CPU architecture, because mixed-architecture clusters are also unsupported.

instruction: Procurement wants to buy whatever servers are cheapest this quarter to grow our SUSE Virtualization cluster. What hardware consistency rules should I give them?
reference: Ask for CPUs with the same specifications as the existing nodes, because live migration checks CPU compatibility and blocks moves between incompatible hosts. Each server must also have a unique product_uuid (/sys/class/dmi/id/product_uuid) to avoid live migration errors.

instruction: We have exactly three SUSE Virtualization nodes and one is going down for a firmware update. Are we still within the fault tolerance limit?
reference: Yes. With three management nodes the cluster tolerates the failure of one node, because etcd keeps quorum with two of three. Do not take a second management node down at the same time.

instruction: A small edge box will be added to an existing SUSE Virtualization cluster purely to keep etcd quorum. Which installer mode and role should be selected, and what must be supplied?
reference: Choose `Join an existing Harvester cluster` and supply the existing cluster's VIP and cluster token. Then select the Witness Role, which limits the node to being an etcd-only witness. The other roles are Default, Management and Worker.

instruction: Our network team plans to renumber the server VLAN next year. What happens to SUSE Virtualization nodes, which currently use DHCP?
reference: Node IPs cannot be changed during the cluster's lifecycle, so renumbering is not supported. A node whose IP changes cannot rejoin the cluster and might break it. Keep DHCP reservations that always return the same IP, with the routers option set for the default route.

instruction: Network design question: we want the SUSE Virtualization VIP on a separate routed management subnet from the node NICs. Is that allowed?
reference: No. The VIP must be in the same subnet as the node management interfaces, and all of those interfaces must be on the same layer-2 segment, because the VIP relies on ARP. It must also be different from every node IP.

instruction: We're moving the SUSE Virtualization VIP to DHCP with a reservation. Which kubectl query gives me the MAC address to reserve?
reference: Run `kubectl get svc -n kube-system ingress-expose -ojsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.kube-vip\.io/hwaddr}'` on a management node. It prints the `kube-vip.io/hwaddr` MAC to use in the static MAC-to-IP mapping.

instruction: After maintenance I suspect the SUSE Virtualization VIP moved to a different server. What kubectl query tells me the current owner?
reference: Run `kubectl -n kube-system get svc ingress-expose -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.kube-vip\.io/vipHost}'`. It prints the node holding the VIP. Alternatively, run `ip address show mgmt-br` on each management node and look for the VIP address.

instruction: I need a shell on one of the SUSE Virtualization hosts to check logs. Which account and command do I use?
reference: Connect as the `rancher` user with `ssh rancher@node-ip`, using the password or SSH key set during installation. Then use `sudo` or `sudo -i` for privileged commands; no password is required.

instruction: I'm writing automation against the SUSE Virtualization Kubernetes API and need admin credentials. Where is the kubeconfig file on the hosts?
reference: On a management node, become root with `sudo su` and run `cat /etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml` to get the kubeconfig. You can also download it from the Support page of the UI.

instruction: The person who set up our SUSE Virtualization cluster left, and the UI admin password is lost. We still have SSH access to the nodes. What do we run?
reference: Become root on a management node and run `kubectl -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password`. It prints a new password for the default administrator.
expect_command: kubectl -n cattle-system exec $(kubectl --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG -n cattle-system get pods -l app=rancher --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{ print $1 }') -c rancher -- reset-password

instruction: The SUSE Virtualization console is still showing setup progress and I want an API-level confirmation that the control plane is up. Which request should I send?
reference: Send `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://$VIP/v1/harvester/readyz` using the cluster token and the real VIP, with `-k` if the certificate is self-signed. A ready control plane returns `{"ready":true,...}`.

instruction: Half our SUSE Virtualization hosts have their data NICs in different slots from the rest. How do cluster networks handle that?
reference: Create one custom cluster network and add a separate network configuration for each group of hosts. Each configuration selects its own nodes and uplink NICs, with bond options (default active-backup). All configurations in the cluster network must use the same MTU. The cluster network is active only on hosts covered by a configuration, and the built-in `mgmt` network stays enabled everywhere.

instruction: I need a VM to sit directly on VLAN 120 of our datacenter network. What do I configure in SUSE Virtualization?
reference: Create a VM network under Networks > VM Networks with type L2VlanNetwork, mode Access, VLAN ID 120, and the cluster network whose uplink carries that VLAN. Then attach it on the VM's Networks tab. The uplink switch ports must be trunk ports that pass VLAN 120 tagged.

instruction: A developer put a database VM on the default management network and its address keeps changing and is unreachable from the office. What should they do instead?
reference: On the management network, a VM's IP is reachable only from the cluster nodes and changes after a reboot. Attach the VM to a VLAN or untagged network for external access with a stable address. Note that management network interfaces also use MTU 1450.

instruction: We set jumbo frames on the management interface in the SUSE Virtualization config file at install time. Which kubectl command makes VM networks on mgmt use it?
reference: Run `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"` with the MTU you installed. The value must match `install.management_interface` `mtu`, and all nodes must use the same MTU; otherwise VM networks on `mgmt` default to 1500.

instruction: A new admin asks where in SUSE Virtualization they pick the OS image and the VLAN for a VM they're building. What do I tell them?
reference: In the VM create form on the Virtual Machines page, they select the image on the Volumes tab, where the first disk becomes the root disk.
