They attach the VLAN network on the Networks tab, where the management network is added by default and can be removed. CPU, memory and SSH keys are on the Basics tab.

instruction: Ops wants a VM to only start and stop when they press the buttons in SUSE Virtualization, never automatically. Which setting?
reference: Set the run strategy to `Manual`. The VM instance is then controlled only by the start, stop and restart actions. The default is `RerunOnFailure`, which respawns failed instances automatically.

instruction: We have a golden qcow2 on a laptop and a nightly-updated URL from a vendor. Which is the safer source for a SUSE Virtualization image?
reference: Upload the fixed qcow2 file, since qcow2, raw and ISO local uploads are supported. Avoid URLs whose content changes, such as daily builds. Longhorn re-downloads the URL to self-heal lost backing-image replicas, and changed content causes a checksum mismatch.

instruction: The IP column for one of our SUSE Virtualization VMs is blank and I suspect the guest agent. Which kubectl query proves it?
reference: Run `kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'`. If `guest-agent` is missing from the output, the `qemu-guest-agent` package is not installed; enable Install guest agent in the VM's Cloud Config.

instruction: I added a package list to the Cloud Config of a SUSE Virtualization VM that has been running for weeks. What must I run inside the guest before rebooting?
reference: Run `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*` inside the guest, then restart the VM. cloud-init runs only on first boot, so clearing its directory makes it run again and apply the new Cloud Config.

instruction: I need to move one specific SUSE Virtualization VM off a host before replacing a disk, without shutting it down. What are the UI steps?
reference: On the Virtual Machines page, select the VM and choose ⋮ > Migrate. Pick the target node and click Apply. If the migration hangs, ⋮ > Abort Migration stops it. Migrate is unavailable on single-node clusters, for non-migratable VMs, or when a migration is already pending.

instruction: Before a rolling host patch, I need to know which of our SUSE Virtualization VMs will need downtime. What makes a VM unable to live-migrate?
reference: Plan downtime for VMs with host device passthrough (PCI, vGPU or USB), VMs bound to one node by a node selector, and VMs whose scheduling rules match only one node, such as a cluster network that exists on a single node. These are non-migratable and must be shut down.

instruction: Migrations of a 16 GiB VM keep failing after about forty minutes. What limit is it hitting, and where is it tuned?
reference: The completion timeout is 150 seconds per GiB by default, so a 16 GiB VM is aborted after 2400 seconds (40 minutes). Tune `completionTimeoutPerGiB` (and `progressTimeout`, default 150 s) in the `kubevirt-migration` setting, or enable `allowAutoConverge` so the migration can converge.

instruction: I want to cap per-migration bandwidth on our SUSE Virtualization 1.8 cluster. Where should that change go, and what precautions apply?
reference: Set `bandwidthPerMigration` in the `kubevirt-migration` setting, not in the `kubevirt` object, because the setting's whole JSON overwrites `spec.configuration.migrations`. Save it only when no migrations are in progress.

instruction: We added newer servers to our SUSE Virtualization cluster and VMs started on them can't migrate back to the old ones. Which object do I edit to standardize the CPU model?
reference: Edit the KubeVirt object with `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system` and add `spec.configuration.cpuModel` set to a model that all nodes support. Restart the VMs afterwards. Alternatively, set `spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.model` on individual VMs.

instruction: A VM tied to a host-attached dongle must stay on its current SUSE Virtualization host. During host maintenance it should power off and come back on that same host afterwards. How do I set that up?
reference: Label the VM with `harvesterhci.io/maintain-mode-strategy` set to `ShutdownAndRestartAfterDisable`. It shuts down when Maintenance Mode is enabled and restarts on the same node when Maintenance Mode is disabled. Other VMs keep the default `Migrate` behavior.

instruction: We want nightly copies of our SUSE Virtualization VMs to land on an on-prem MinIO bucket. Is that possible, and where is it configured?
reference: Yes. An S3-compatible server can be the backup target. Configure it at Settings > backup-target with type S3, endpoint, bucket name, region and keys (plus a certificate if self-signed). Backups work only for SUSE Storage (Longhorn) volumes, not external storage.

instruction: For disaster recovery to a second SUSE Virtualization site, should I rely on VM snapshots or VM backups?
reference: Use VM backups. Snapshots stay inside the source cluster, while backups are written to the external backup target. The second cluster can restore them as new VMs once it is configured with the same backup target.

instruction: We're about to roll out scheduled snapshots for a fleet of Ubuntu 22.04 VMs on SUSE Virtualization. Is there a guest network setting to fix first?
reference: Yes. Set `dhcp-identifier: mac` in the netplan network configuration of each VM before taking backups or snapshots. Otherwise a restored VM keeps the original machine ID and gets the same DHCP IP, causing conflicts.

instruction: I want to keep the last seven daily backups of a VM automatically on SUSE Virtualization. How do I configure that?
reference: Create a schedule on the Virtual Machine Schedules screen with type Backup, the VM, a daily cron expression and Retain set to 7. The interval must be at least one hour. Max Failure sets how many consecutive failures suspend it. Do not use Longhorn recurring jobs; they are not supported.

instruction: Before trusting backup consistency for a busy SUSE Virtualization VM, I want to check by hand that its filesystems can be quiesced. What do I run, and what must I not forget?
reference: From the VM's virt-launcher `compute` container, run `virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` and verify the result. Then always thaw with `virt-freezer --unfreeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` before any other operation.

instruction: We're on SUSE Virtualization v1.7.2 managed by Rancher and want v1.8. What upgrade order and path apply?
reference: Upgrade Rancher first, then upgrade SUSE Virtualization from v1.7.x straight to a v1.8.x release, since one minor step is supported without intermediate patches. Downgrades are not supported, so back up VMs before you start.

instruction: I'm preparing a maintenance window for a SUSE Virtualization upgrade. What should I run on each host to confirm the free-space prerequisite, and what's the threshold?
reference: Run `df -h /usr/local/` on each node. Every node needs at least 30 GiB of free system partition space; otherwise the upgrade is denied.

instruction: During SUSE Virtualization upgrade preparation, node-2 is reported to exceed the 85% image GC threshold. What's the quickest documented remedy before retrying?
reference: On node-2, run `crictl rmi --prune` to remove unused container images, then start a new upgrade. The 85% check prevents the kubelet from garbage-collecting the newly loaded upgrade images.

instruction: We have several VMs with PCI passthrough and want them back automatically after our SUSE Virtualization upgrade. Which setting do we change?
reference: Set `restoreVM` to `true` in the `upgrade-config` setting before upgrading. Non-migratable VMs are then shut down during the node upgrade and the previously running ones are restarted after the upgrade completes. With the default `false`, you must stop them yourself and they are not restarted.

instruction: The SUSE Virtualization upgrade has been stuck in system services for hours and I want to cancel it cleanly. Which kubectl query identifies the object to delete?
reference: As root on a control-plane node, run `kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true` and delete the Upgrade CR it lists. Then resume paused ManagedCharts. Generate a support bundle before stopping.

instruction: The second node of our SUSE Virtualization cluster has been in post-drain for a long time. What command shows the node jobs, and is restarting the upgrade an option?
reference: Run `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node` and check the post-drain job logs. Do not restart an upgrade that is failing or stuck in Phase 4 (node upgrades) unless SUSE Support instructs you to.

instruction: We have two strong servers and one small box at a third site. Can the small box keep quorum for a SUSE Virtualization cluster without running VMs?
reference: Yes. Install it as a witness node by choosing Witness Role when it joins the cluster. It acts only as an etcd member, stores no data, and gives a supported two-management-plus-one-witness layout. Only one witness is allowed per cluster, and it still needs to meet etcd hardware recommendations.

instruction: We just built a three-node SUSE Virtualization cluster where one node is the witness. What storage change should we make before creating VMs?
reference: Create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2. Only the two management nodes store data, so the default `harvester-longhorn` StorageClass, with 3 replicas, would leave volumes Degraded.

instruction: An operator migrated a VM to 'harvester-node-1' and it failed; that node was installed with the witness role. What's the guidance?
reference: Do not select the witness node as a migration target. It can appear in the target list, but migrations to it fail because it only acts as an etcd member. Migrate to a management or worker node instead.

instruction: I added an NVIDIA card to a SUSE Virtualization host and want a VM to use it exclusively. What are the steps from enabling to first boot?
reference: Enable the `pcidevices-controller` add-on, then on Advanced > PCI Devices select the card and click Enable Passthrough. Attach it in the VM's Edit Config > PCI Devices, save, and restart the VM. The device is bound to `vfio-pci`, so install the NVIDIA driver inside the guest.

instruction: We want to share one NVIDIA data-center GPU between several VMs on SUSE Virtualization 1.8. Which add-ons and screens are involved?
reference: Enable the `pcidevices-controller` and `nvidia-driver-toolkit` add-ons. Enable the GPU on Advanced > SR-IOV GPU Devices, then choose a profile for each vGPU on the vGPU Devices screen. In v1.8, attach each vGPU to a VM by passing through the PCIDevice with the same name as the VGPUDevice.

instruction: Security wants to know what has to be opened in the firewall so our SUSE Virtualization cluster shows up under Rancher's Virtualization Management, and how the import is started.
reference: Open TCP port 443 from every SUSE Virtualization node to the Rancher load balancer. Start the import in Rancher under Virtualization Management > Import Existing, then complete the registration guide in the SUSE Virtualization UI, which sets `cluster-registration-url`.

instruction: Our team proposes running the production Rancher instance for SUSE Virtualization as a single Docker container on a utility VM. Is that acceptable?
reference: No. For production, Rancher should run on a dedicated, high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes. Docker installs are only for quick evaluation and testing, because the environment may be damaged and unrecoverable.

instruction: I want Rancher to spin up a three-node RKE2 cluster as VMs on our SUSE Virtualization cluster. What prerequisites should I have ready?
reference: Prepare a cloud image (not an ISO), a VLAN network with DHCP (or the Managed DHCP add-on), and a Harvester cloud credential created as Imported Harvester Cluster. Then create the cluster in Rancher with the Harvester node driver, which is enabled by default.

instruction: We switched to a slimmer cloud image for Rancher-provisioned clusters on SUSE Virtualization and provisioning now hangs. What changed in the node driver that matters here?
reference: Since Harvester node driver v0.6.3, `qemu-guest-agent` is no longer injected automatically. If the slimmer image lacks it, add a User Data cloud-config that installs `qemu-guest-agent` and runs `systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service`; otherwise provisioning does not succeed.

instruction: A VM attached to cluster network 'storage-net' shows Unschedulable with 0 nodes matching node affinity. What is the root cause and fix in SUSE Virtualization?
reference: SUSE Virtualization added an automatic affinity rule for the label `network.harvesterhci.io/storage-net`, and no active node carries it. Make sure active nodes have the `storage-net` cluster network set up through a network configuration so they get the label, and the pending pod will schedule.

instruction: In SUSE Virtualization, VM 'app01' is Off, its virt-launcher pod shows Completed, and the UI offers no way to start it. What do I run?
reference: Force delete the completed pod: `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force` (the pod is named like `virt-launcher-app01-xxxxx`). After it is deleted, the Start button becomes visible again.

instruction: A colleague claims NeuVector is a single agent binary. What are its actual building blocks?
reference: SUSE Security (NeuVector) is not a single agent: it consists of four security container types, the Controller, Enforcer, Manager and Scanner, plus an Updater container that refreshes the CVE database.

instruction: Our automation team wants to script against SUSE Security. Which component should they talk to, and how should it be deployed for resilience?
reference: Automation should talk to the Controller, which provides the REST APIs (the console also uses them) and manages the Enforcers. Deploy multiple Controllers for high availability; the Kubernetes production sample defaults to 3 Controllers.

instruction: Why does SUSE Security deploy one of its containers on every single node?
reference: That is the Enforcer. It enforces the security policies locally on each host, so one Enforcer must be deployed per node, typically as a DaemonSet.

instruction: Which SUSE Security container serves the browser console, and what should I watch out for when making it highly available?
reference: The Manager serves the HTTPS-only web console. It is stateless, but running more than one Manager behind a load balancer is not recommended because of potential session state issues.

instruction: Our registry has thousands of images and scans take forever. Which SUSE Security component do we scale and how is work shared?
reference: Scale the Scanner replicaset. Scanners do the vulnerability and compliance scanning, and the Controller distributes scan jobs across all available scanners in a round-robin fashion.

instruction: Explain how a fresh vulnerability feed ends up in our NeuVector scanners each day.
reference: The Updater cron job (default schedule "0 0 * * *", midnight daily) restarts the scanner deployment, which forces a pull of the latest scanner image. That image contains the newest CVE database.

instruction: I'm scaling the controller deployment to 2 replicas to save resources. Any problem with that?
reference: Two is not recommended. Controllers use the RAFT consensus protocol to elect a leader, so the number of active Controllers should be odd, for example 3, 5 or 7.

instruction: Give me the per-component CPU and RAM baseline for planning a NeuVector install.
reference: Controller: 1 vCPU, 2GB (3 for HA, odd only). Enforcer: 1+ vCPU, 1GB, one per node. Scanner: 1 vCPU, 2GB (2+ for HA/performance). Manager: 1 vCPU, 1GB.

instruction: Our biggest container image is 4GB. What memory should the SUSE Security scanner get?
reference: Apply the documented rule for images over 1GB: largest image size plus 0.5GB, so about 4.5GB for a 4GB image. The scanner expands the image in memory during the scan.

instruction: I made a group with label criteria and want to switch it to Monitor, but can't. What's going on?
reference: Custom groups do not have a protection mode; only learned 'nv' groups and the 'Nodes' group can be in Discover, Monitor or Protect. Change the mode on the underlying 'nv.' groups.

instruction: After install, why is SUSE Security creating lots of network rules on its own?
reference: Groups start in Discover mode by default. In Discover, SUSE Security observes container conversations and automatically builds allow-list network rules and process profile rules for normal behaviour.

instruction: If I switch a group from Discover to Monitor, will it keep learning new connections?
reference: No. In Monitor mode SUSE Security creates no new rules; it detects and alerts on violations of the existing policy without blocking. You can still add rules manually.

instruction: What is the practical difference between Monitor and Protect for an unknown process starting in a container?
reference: Monitor only alerts on the unauthorized process. Protect blocks it: in Protect mode Enforcers deny network violations and also block unauthorized processes and file access.

instruction: Our team wants to go straight from install to Protect on a payment service. What would you advise?
reference: Don't skip the learning phase. Exercise the service in Discover (several hours to a few days), review rules, then use Monitor to find violations and convert them to allow rules before switching to Protect.

instruction: Group A is Monitor, group B is Protect. A disallowed connection goes from B to A. Blocked or not?
reference: Not blocked. The effective mode for network rules is the least restrictive of the two groups, so Protect to Monitor is treated as Monitor and only alerted.

instruction: Two of my network rules overlap and the wrong one seems to apply. How does SUSE Security pick?
reference: Rules are enforced top to bottom in the displayed order, so the higher rule wins; move the intended rule above the other and click Save/Deploy. Connections matching no rule default to Deny.

instruction: Our app must call a payment API at a fixed hostname outside the cluster, and the group is in Protect. How do I permit just that?
reference: Create a custom group with address criteria for the API's DNS name, then add an Allow network rule from the app's group to that group (optionally limited by port or protocol) and Deploy it.

instruction: Since we preserved client IPs on our ingress, Protect-mode apps get violations from 'external'. What's the documented toggle?
reference: Disable 'X-Forwarded-For based policy match' in Settings → Configuration. It is on by default and makes SUSE Security treat connections as external based on the X-Forwarded-For header.

instruction: I set the nodes group to Protect expecting host-level firewalling, but a bad host connection only raised an alert. Is that a bug?
reference: No, that is documented behaviour. Network violations for the 'nodes' group are never blocked, even in Protect mode; only process violations are blocked on nodes.

instruction: We upgraded docs knowledge from 5.5. Our trainer says zero-drift is always the default. Correct?
reference: Only for older versions. Zero-drift was the default in NeuVector 5.6.0 and older; starting from 5.6.1, Basic is the default for new deployments.

instruction: Explain zero-drift to a security auditor in two sentences.
reference: Zero-drift allows only processes that descend from the original container image's parent process and blocks file changes or new files from being installed, without needing a learned allow-list. It alerts in Discover/Monitor mode and blocks in Protect mode.

instruction: A team disabled zero-drift on a brand new group and moved it to Monitor; now they get alerts for every process. Explain.
reference: Disabling zero-drift switches the group to Basic protection, which relies on the group's process/file rules. With no rules in place, all activity is alerted in Monitor mode; learn rules in Discover or add them first.

instruction: A healthcheck script uses a port scanner; it is flagged even though the group was learning. What do I do?
reference: Port scanners like nmap are built-in suspicious processes and are not learned in Discover mode. Add an explicit allow process rule for it in that group.

instruction: Compliance asks us to prevent any tampering with /etc/hosts in all pods using NeuVector file rules. Feasible?
reference: Not with blocking: /etc/hosts is a predefined monitored file, and SUSE Security only alerts on modifications to predefined files. Blocking is available only for custom files/directories in non-system containers.

instruction: Security wants every image in our Harbor project re-evaluated whenever the vulnerability feed changes. Which registry option?
reference: Enable 'Rescan after CVE DB update' for that registry in Assets → Registries; by default only new or updated images are scanned.

instruction: Our registry entry won't save without a filter. What should we put to cover everything in a private Nexus?
reference: A repository filter is mandatory. Use * or *:* to scan all tags; that works for all registry types except the public Docker registry.

instruction: Scans of our private Quay are stuck failing. What are the two usual culprits per the docs?
reference: Registry authentication errors, or the controller being unable to access the registry from the cluster.

instruction: I want new pods checked for CVEs the moment they start. What do I enable?
reference: Enable Auto-Scan in the Vulnerabilities tab under Assets → Containers (or Nodes). It scans running and newly started assets and rescans after CVE database updates.

instruction: I removed the updater by mistake during cleanup. How do I put it back?
reference: Recreate it from the sample yaml with `kubectl create -f neuvector-updater.yaml`; it runs nightly and restarts the scanners to pull the latest CVE database.

instruction: After a fresh install, no admission webhook for NeuVector appears in the cluster. Is the install broken?
reference: Not necessarily. Admission Control is disabled by default; the neuvector-validating-admission-webhook ValidatingWebhookConfiguration is created only after you enable it in Policy → Admission Control.

instruction: Write the kubectl check that proves NeuVector's admission integration is registered with the API server.
reference: `kubectl get ValidatingWebhookConfiguration neuvector-validating-admission-webhook` should list the neuvector-validating-admission-webhook resource once Admission Control is enabled.

instruction: We want to trial admission rules for a week without breaking deployments. Which mode?
reference: Use Monitor mode: denied decisions are only alerted and resources are still created. Switch to Protect when you want denied deployments blocked.

instruction: A CRD deny rule and a user-defined allow rule both match a deployment. Which wins?
reference: The CRD deny rule. CRD-applied rules (allow then deny) are evaluated before user-defined allow and deny rules, and the first matching stage determines the action.

instruction: Developers are pulling images from a registry we never configured for scanning to dodge CVE rules. How do we close that gap?
reference: Add an admission rule with the 'Image scanned' criterion. Scan-based criteria are skipped for unscanned images, so requiring a scan stops that bypass.

instruction: Our apiserver says it's failing open on the NeuVector webhook because the lookup returned no such host. Diagnose.
reference: The kube-apiserver cannot resolve the neuvector-svc-admission-webhook service name. Fix DNS resolution of that service from the API server.

instruction: Admission control can't create its webhook; I suspect RBAC. What do I inspect first?
reference: Inspect `kubectl get clusterrole neuvector-binding-admission -o json` and verify the verbs get, list, watch, create, update and delete are present.

instruction: Auditors want a DISA STIG view of our cluster from NeuVector. Is there a template and where do I get the report?
reference: Yes, DISA STIG is a built-in compliance template (with PCI, GDPR, HIPAA, NIST and PCIv4). Filter by it in Security Risks → Compliance and export the report.

instruction: We are rolling SUSE Security onto a K3s edge cluster via Rancher Apps. What runtime value and namespace should we expect?
reference: Select the K3s value for the container run-time (containerd is for RKE2, docker for RKE). The app installs into the cattle-neuvector-system namespace.

instruction: Security review flagged default credentials on our new SUSE Security console. What's documented?
reference: The default login is admin/admin, and you are prompted to change it at first login. Log in directly as admin and set a strong password, or supply the admin password via a ConfigMap secret at deployment.

instruction: Setting up a fresh workstation to manage NeuVector via Helm with Rancher charts. What repo command goes first?
reference: `helm repo add rancher-charts https://charts.rancher.io/` and then `helm repo update`.

instruction: Write out the Helm step that lays down SUSE Security's custom resource definitions on a Rancher cluster.
reference: `helm install neuvector-crd --namespace cattle-neuvector-system --create-namespace rancher-charts/neuvector-crd --version={chart-version}` (substitute the chart version compatible with your Rancher release).

instruction: CIS-hardened RKE2 blocks the NeuVector enforcer from starting. What namespace label is required?
reference: Allow privileged pods in the namespace with `kubectl label namespace cattle-neuvector-system pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged`.

instruction: Our values.yaml for Rancher integration is ready. Provide the install line for the core SUSE Security chart.
reference: `helm install neuvector --namespace cattle-neuvector-system --create-namespace rancher-charts/neuvector --version={chart-version} -f values.yaml`
expect_command: helm install neuvector --namespace cattle-neuvector-system --create-namespace rancher-charts/neuvector --version={chart-version} -f values.yaml

instruction: Ops asks which node port they must open in the firewall for the SUSE Security console. How do I find it?
reference: Run `kubectl get svc --namespace cattle-neuvector-system neuvector-service-webui` and read the NodePort mapped from 8443 in the PORT(S) column.

instruction: Our disconnected site has a Harbor registry. In broad steps, how do we get SUSE Security there?
reference: Use Helm, Skopeo and zstd: pull the chart, list its images with helm template, save them with skopeo, compress with tar/zstd, carry the bundle in, load images into Harbor with skopeo, then helm install with the registry values pointing to Harbor.

instruction: I'm preparing a USB transfer for a disconnected cluster. Which Helm command fetches the SUSE Security chart file?
reference: `helm pull neuvector/core -d neuvector` (after adding the neuvector repo and running helm repo update).

instruction: The controller deployment shows 0/3 ready and I want the cluster's own record of what happened. Which command?
reference: `kubectl get events -n neuvector`

instruction: I need verbose controller logs cluster-wide for an hour. What do I type in the NeuVector CLI?
reference: After login, `set system controller_debug -c all`; remember to switch debug off afterwards.

instruction: Before opening a case, what diagnostic file can I grab from the NeuVector console itself?
reference: The support log: Settings → Configuration, then Collect Log.

instruction: We're about to do rolling OS reboots across the cluster. How do I guarantee two SUSE Security controllers stay up?
reference: Create the PDB from the sample nv_pdb.yaml (minAvailable: 2, app: neuvector-controller-pod) with `kubectl create -f nv_pdb.yaml`.

instruction: What storage do I have to provision so SUSE Security can restore its policy after a total cluster loss?
reference: An RWX (ReadWriteMany) persistent volume of 1Gi or more, mounted at /var/neuvector in the controller pods; without it configuration and policy are not persisted.

instruction: Upgrade checklist item: we're moving controllers from 5.5.x to 5.6.2. What do we need to do with the scanners?
reference: Restart or redeploy the existing scanner pods after the controller upgrade; they cache the old capability response and otherwise won't recognise critical-level severity.

instruction: A team wants to write one policy that applies across namespaces. Which NeuVector CRD kind fits, and what can't they then do in the UI?
reference: Use NvClusterSecurityRule, which is cluster-scoped (NvSecurityRule is namespace-scoped). If it sets a policymode, that mode can't be changed in the console; change it in the CRD.

instruction: Our GitOps job needs the exact kubectl invocation to roll out a changed SUSE Security policy-as-code file.
reference: `kubectl apply -f <crdrule.yaml>`

instruction: Automation should bootstrap users and syslog for SUSE Security before first login. Which command and resource?
reference: Fill in the sample initcfg.yaml (ConfigMap neuvector-init) and run `kubectl create -f initcfg.yaml` before the controllers start.

instruction: A colleague handed me a fresh SLES 15 SP7 VM and an SCC registration code. What single command links it to SUSE Customer Center?
reference: Run `sudo SUSEConnect -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS` with your registration code and the e-mail address of your SUSE account. This registers SLES and its default Basesystem and Server Applications modules and adds the repositories.

instruction: We mirror updates through an internal RMT host. How do I point SUSEConnect at it while registering a SLES 15 machine?
reference: Pass the server URL with `--url` during registration: `sudo SUSEConnect -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS --url "https://suse_register.example.com/"`, replacing the example URL with your RMT host.

instruction: Before enabling anything extra on a SLES 15 server, I want an overview of every add-on module SUSE offers for it. What do I run?
reference: Run `sudo SUSEConnect --list-extensions`. It lists available modules and extensions, marks activated ones, and prints the activation command for each.

instruction: Our CI builders run SLES 15 SP7 on x86_64 and need the module that ships container tooling. Which SUSEConnect call turns it on?
reference: Activate the Containers Module with `SUSEConnect -p sle-module-containers/15.7/x86_64` (as root). Then install the packages you need with zypper.

instruction: My manager wants the Workstation Extension on a SLES 15 SP7 desktop. Will our server registration code cover it?
reference: No. The Workstation Extension is an extension, and all extensions require an additional registration code. Activate it with `SUSEConnect -p sle-we/15.7/x86_64 -r ADDITIONAL REGCODE` using the extension's code.

instruction: After deactivating the Web and Scripting Module with SUSEConnect, PHP is still on the box. How can I see everything that is now left without a repository?
reference: SUSEConnect does not remove packages when a module is deleted. List the leftover packages with `sudo zypper packages --orphaned`; they no longer receive updates.

instruction: A junior admin proposes trimming every module on a minimal SLES 15 SP7 appliance, including the base one. What's the guidance?
reference: Never delete the Basesystem Module, and keeping the Server Applications Module is recommended too. Remove only the optional modules you don't need.

instruction: We're retiring a SLES 15 host and want its subscription seat freed in SCC. What do I run on the host?
reference: Run `sudo SUSEConnect -d`. This deregisters the system and all its modules and extensions, removes its entry on the registration server, and removes the repositories.

instruction: Will a SUSEConnect package update re-enable the keep-alive timer if I switch it off, and how do I switch it off?
reference: Disable it with `sudo systemctl disable --now suseconnect-keepalive.timer`. After you disable it, later updates to the SUSEConnect package will not re-enable it.

instruction: For a GPU training box on SLES 15 SP7, which SUSEConnect identifier pulls in NVIDIA's CUDA driver repository, and who supports it?
reference: Activate it with `SUSEConnect -p sle-module-NVIDIA-compute/15/x86_64`; the version in the identifier is 15. The module comes from NVIDIA under the CUDA EULA and is not supported by SUSE.

instruction: It's patch Tuesday for our SLES 15 SP7 fleet. What zypper command applies all the official fixes that apply to each host?
reference: Run `sudo zypper patch`. It installs all relevant official patches (except optional and feature ones) and warns before installing a patch that needs a reboot.

instruction: Our auditor wants evidence of which applicable fixes are still missing on a SLES 15 host, without changing anything. Which read-only zypper command produces that?
reference: Run `zypper list-patches`. It lists the patches that apply to the system but are not yet installed, and it does not install anything.

instruction: A security bulletin references CVE-2010-2713. On a SLES server I only want the patch for that entry applied. What's the zypper invocation?
reference: Run `sudo zypper patch --cve=CVE-2010-2713`. It installs only the patches for that CVE.

instruction: Explain to a Debian admin moving to SLES when to reach for 'zypper update' instead of 'zypper patch'.
reference: Use `zypper patch` for official patches; it reports a conflict if a vulnerable package can't be updated. Use `zypper update` when a repository has new package versions but no patches. Note that it skips problematic packages, such as locked ones, without reporting a conflict.

instruction: Patching finished on a SLES database host and I'd like to restart only what's necessary. Which zypper subcommand shows stale processes?
reference: Run `zypper ps`. It lists processes still using deleted files and, where known, the service to restart.

instruction: I added a repo yesterday and today zypper search can't see a package that is definitely in it, even after a normal refresh. What's the stronger fix?
reference: Run `sudo zypper refresh -fdb`. It forces a complete refresh and rebuilds the database, including a forced download of the raw metadata.

instruction: Our golden SLES 15 image never sees any patches when we run zypper patch on it. What's the most likely missing step?
reference: The image is probably not registered. The official update repository is only available after registration, so register with `sudo SUSEConnect -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS` (or YaST) and patch again.

instruction: Coming from SLES, I'm surprised my edge box on SUSE Linux Micro refuses package changes to /usr. What's the model there?
reference: SUSE Linux Micro has a read-only root file system. Changes are made with `transactional-update` into a new snapshot, which becomes active after a reboot.

instruction: On a SUSE Linux Micro edge gateway I need the tcpdump package for debugging. What's the supported way to add it?
reference: Use `sudo transactional-update pkg install package_name` with tcpdump as the package name, then reboot into the new snapshot.

instruction: Monthly maintenance on a fleet of SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 nodes: which transactional-update subcommand applies the released fixes?
reference: Run `transactional-update patch` as root on each node. It installs available patches into a new snapshot, and you reboot to activate it.

instruction: I just flashed SUSE Linux Micro onto a mini PC and have an SCC code. What registers it from the shell?
reference: Run `transactional-update register -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS` as root, with your registration code and SUSE account e-mail.

instruction: On a SUSE Linux Micro test box I patched, then installed htop, then rebooted, and the patches seem gone. What happened, and how do I avoid it?
reference: Each transactional-update run without `--continue` creates an independent snapshot from the current root, so the htop snapshot didn't include the patches. Use `--continue` (or one `transactional-update shell` session) to stack changes before a reboot.

instruction: I need to add two repos and four packages on a SUSE Linux Micro node in one go and then reboot once. Which transactional-update mode suits that?
reference: Use `transactional-update shell`. Make all the changes with zypper inside it, `exit`, then reboot once to activate the single snapshot.

instruction: Yesterday's automatic update on a SUSE Linux Micro kiosk introduced a regression; the device still boots. How do I go back to snapshot 42?
reference: Run `sudo transactional-update rollback snapshot_number` with 42 as the snapshot number (check it with `sudo snapper list`), then reboot.

instruction: Our change board forbids unattended updates on production SUSE Linux Micro nodes. Which unit do I disable, and how?
reference: Disable `transactional-update.timer`: `sudo systemctl --now disable transactional-update.timer`.

instruction: A colleague's install script under transactional-update run uses relative paths and writes logs to /var/log/myapp. Which two environment details will trip it up?
reference: In the transactional-update environment, the working directory is `/`, not the caller's directory. `/var` is not in the snapshot and is not accessible, so writing to `/var/log/myapp` fails.

instruction: I want the web console on a SUSE Linux Micro node built from the minimal base image. What do I run first?
reference: Install the Cockpit pattern with `transactional-update pkg install -t pattern cockpit` as root, then reboot into the new snapshot.

instruction: After installing the Cockpit pattern and rebooting, what makes the machine serve the web console, and at what address?
reference: Run `systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket`. Then open `https://IP_ADDRESS_OF_MACHINE:9090`.

instruction: Locally curl to :9090 works on my SUSE Linux Micro host, but nobody on the LAN can reach the console. Which firewalld rule fixes it?
reference: Allow the cockpit service: `firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=cockpit`, then `firewall-cmd --reload`.

instruction: Our runbook says to sign in to the Micro web console as root, but the login page rejects it on a freshly installed node. How should we adjust the runbook?
reference: On new SUSE Linux Micro installs, Cockpit disallows root password login by default. Use an unprivileged user and unlock administrative access with the root password, preferably with 2FA. Removing root from `/etc/cockpit/disallowed-users` is possible but strongly discouraged.

instruction: A SLES 16.0 server was installed without the web console. Which zypper command adds it afterwards?
reference: Run `sudo zypper in -t pattern cockpit`, then enable it with `sudo systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket`.

instruction: For a build stage that has to install extra tools with zypper from SUSE's free repository, which general-purpose SUSE Linux BCI fits, and what's its main drawback?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Base: it includes Zypper and the free SLE_BCI repository. Its drawback is that it is the largest general-purpose BCI (about 135 MB for 15.7).

instruction: I want a SUSE Linux BCI that's smaller than base yet still lets me drop in a couple of RPMs at build time with rpm itself. Which one, and what's the catch?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Minimal: it has rpm but no Zypper. The catch is that rpm has no repository support or automatic dependency resolution, so you resolve dependencies manually.

instruction: Our Rust service is compiled in a bci-base build stage into one self-contained binary. Which general-purpose SUSE Linux BCI does SUSE suggest for the runtime stage, given there's no package manager needed?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Micro. It has no Zypper or rpm and is intended for deploying binaries that bundle all their dependencies, typically from multi-stage builds.

instruction: Legal won't let us ship anything GPLv3 in our appliance container, and we want it tiny. Which SUSE Linux BCI meets that, and what compatibility issue should devs expect?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox: it contains no GPLv3-licensed software and is about 12 MB. Its BusyBox tools differ from GNU Coreutils (and there's no bash), so some scripts may need changes.

instruction: A startup wants to base its open-source product image on SUSE's container images and push it to Docker Hub without buying anything. Is that allowed?
reference: Yes. SUSE Linux BCIs don't require a subscription to run or distribute, and their permissive EULA allows redistributing custom images built on them.

instruction: We're writing our container build standards. What tag policy does SUSE advise for bci images, and why now in particular?
reference: Pin explicit version tags (for example `registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7` or a 16.x tag) instead of `:latest`. The `:latest` tag across the BCI family is migrating from SLES 15 to SUSE Linux 16 image by image.

instruction: Before approving bci-base:15.7 for production, compliance wants proof of its SUSE support level straight from the registry metadata. What command shows it?
reference: Run `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`. An output of `"l3"` means the image is fully supported.

instruction: A team building Java services asks whether SUSE has a BCI with the JDK compiler, not just the runtime. What exists?
reference: Yes. The openjdk BCI ships the OpenJDK runtime, and openjdk-devel adds the development part of OpenJDK, with jshell as the default entry point. Both are Development Stack BCIs built on BCI-Base.

instruction: Our build server isn't registered with SCC, but we have an LTSS registration code and need an LTSS image from SUSE Registry. How do we authenticate?
reference: Log in with the literal user `regcode` and the code as the password: `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`.

instruction: I'm scripting chart pulls from SUSE's curated app catalog. What does the Helm authentication step look like?
reference: Run `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>` with an access token (user account) or a service account secret.

instruction: Our platform team needs a reusable pull credential in the cluster so workloads can use SUSE's curated container images. What single kubectl command creates it?
reference: Run `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=<your-username-or-sa-username> --docker-password=<access-token-or-sa-secret>`.

instruction: Show me how to deploy Redis from SUSE's curated catalog using the pull secret we already created, called application-collection.
reference: Run `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`.

instruction: I belong to two SUSE orgs, one with a Prime subscription and one with Prime plus SUSE AI. Which Application Collection credential type sees content from both, and which one is limited?
reference: A user account (username plus access token) inherits the subscriptions of all your organizations, so it can pull both. A service account is tied to one organization and gets only that organization's subscriptions.

instruction: We mirrored SUSE Application Collection images into Harbor and charts deploy into team namespaces. What two settings and which precondition matter?
reference: Set `global.imageRegistry` to the mirror and `global.imagePullSecrets` to the mirror's pull secret. The secret must already exist in each target namespace.

instruction: Our Rancher Prime contract is active; can we go straight to helm-installing Ollama and Open WebUI for SUSE AI?
reference: Not by itself. The SUSE AI entitlement is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime. Once the check at https://apps.rancher.io/ passes, you can pull the SUSE AI charts and images from SUSE Application Collection.

instruction: Planning SUSE AI 1.0 on bare metal: which OS options and which Kubernetes does SUSE's guide steer us to?
reference: SLES 15 SP6 (traditional) or SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 (immutable, transactional), with SUSE Rancher Prime: RKE2 as the Kubernetes distribution.

instruction: Architecture review question: how many Kubernetes clusters, and for what roles, does SUSE advise for a production SUSE AI rollout?
reference: Three separate clusters: one for Rancher, one for SUSE Observability, and one for the AI Library workloads. SUSE strongly recommends this separation for production.

instruction: Setting up the namespace for SUSE AI Library apps: besides the Application Collection credential, what Kubernetes secret is needed and with which odd-looking username?
reference: A SUSE Registry pull secret whose username is `regcode`: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`.

instruction: Our RKE2 cluster mixes T4 GPU workers with plain workers. What labeling command from the SUSE AI guide should I run on the GPU workers before setting nodeSelector?
reference: Run `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu` for each GPU node, then use `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia-gpu` in the chart values.

instruction: vLLM chart values: what resource stanza makes Kubernetes hand the pod one GPU from the NVIDIA operator?
reference: Request the `nvidia.com/gpu` resource, for example `requests: nvidia.com/gpu: 1` and `limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1`, and make sure GPU passthrough is enabled in the chart.

instruction: After installing the GPU Operator with driver.enabled false, the node's gpu.deploy.driver label says true. The packages are installed. What's the likely fix?
reference: A value of `true` means the operator did not detect correctly installed drivers; it should be `pre-installed`. The likely cause is that the node wasn't rebooted after installing the driver packages, so reboot and check again.

instruction: I have a fresh SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 host with an L40S. Outline the SUSE AI-documented flow for getting the NVIDIA driver working.
reference: Run `transactional-update shell`. Inside it, add the NVIDIA repository and install the open driver packages (G06 generation) with zypper. Then `exit`, `reboot`, and check with `nvidia-smi`.

instruction: I'm sequencing a SUSE AI install. Which component that used to come bundled now has to go in first on its own, and which LLM runtime comes along with Open WebUI unless I disable it?
reference: cert-manager is no longer part of the Open WebUI chart and must be installed separately first. Ollama is installed by the Open WebUI chart by default unless you disable it in the overrides.

instruction: Our SUSE AI namespace and secrets are ready and ollama_custom_overrides.yaml enables the GPU. What's the Helm call that installs or upgrades Ollama?
reference: Run `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`.
